For over decades, JK Cement has 
grown with quiet conviction, shaped by 
patience, disciplined execution and a deep 
understanding of markets and customer 
needs. We have always believed that 
enduring scale is built on strong foundations 
and thoughtful decisions. Today, as 
opportunities expand, we are building 
on that foundation with greater speed 
and purpose.
DISCIPLINED 
EXECUTION. 
ACCELERATED 
GROWTH.
In the past five years, we have more than doubled our 
production capacity primarily through organic expansion, 
strengthened our presence across strategic regions, 
increased market share. During this time, we have also 
evolved from a pureplay cement manufacturer into 
an integrated building materials company. Today, our 
portfolio spans grey and white cement, wall putty, paints, 
tile adhesives and grouts, gypsum plaster, construction 
chemicals, RMC and allied solutions.
This evolution reflects a consistent execution philosophy: 
build with foresight, operationalise with speed, and grow 
with financial discipline. Strategic capacity additions, 
investments in logistics, green power, and digital capabilities 
have sharpened our competitive edge. Technology and 
digitalisation have become foundational pillars of our 
strategy. Advanced analytics and AI-driven manufacturing 
intelligence optimise our production efficiency. Digital 
channel platforms enhance direct customer engagement 
and real-time responsiveness. Robust cybersecurity 
infrastructure protects our operations and stakeholder 
interests. We have done this while upholding the 
highest level of governance ensuring transparency 
and accountability.  
Growth, for us, has always meant responsible growth. 
We have embedded sustainability into operations through 
renewable energy integration, waste heat recovery, 
improved thermal substitution, and water positivity. Our 
commitment to safety, skill development, and community 
engagement reflects our belief that industrial progress must 
create wider social value.
As we enter the next phase, this approach remains our 
guiding philosophy. Disciplined execution, powered by 
technology and innovation, is now accelerating growth. 
We are building not just faster, but better, with the resilience, 
responsibility, and long-term perspective that have defined 
us for fifty years and will guide us for the fifty years ahead.

About the report
Report overview and approach
Our Integrated Annual Report for FY 2025-26 provides a 
clear and balanced overview of our Company’s strategy, 
performance, governance and outlook. It includes vital 
financial and non-financial disclosures that are relevant to our 
stakeholders and illustrates how our strategic objectives are 
designed to generate long-term value. Additionally,  
it details our approach to navigating risks and adapting to 
shifts in the broader context, ensuring the well-being of all  
our stakeholders.
Integration of the stakeholder priorities
Our value creation approach is shaped by the priorities of 
our stakeholders and enabled by the resources, relationships 
and capabilities we deploy across the business. Financial 
strength and manufacturing scale support disciplined growth 
and operational reliability. People capability and innovation 
strengthen safety, execution excellence, digital readiness 
and product development. Stakeholder relationships 
reinforce trust across markets, communities and institutions. 
Environmental stewardship supports responsible resource 
use, regulatory readiness and long-term resilience.
These resources are interconnected and are addressed 
across our strategy, governance, risk management, materiality 
assessment, performance disclosures and sustainability 
priorities. Presenting them through a stakeholder-led lens 
enables us to show how business decisions translate into 
outcomes for the people and institutions most affected by, 
or connected to our operations.

Materiality
The contents of this report are guided by a structured 
materiality assessment process that identifies the economic, 
environmental, social and governance matters most 
significant to our long-term value creation and stakeholders. 
The assessment is informed by stakeholder engagement, 
management insights, and an evaluation of our impacts, risks 
and opportunities. We prioritise and address these material 
matters throughout the report, linking them to stakeholder 
expectations, strategic priorities, risk management and 
performance outcomes.
Completeness and reporting approach 
We have endeavoured to present a balanced, complete and 
reliable account of our performance during FY 2025-26. 
The report includes both achievements and areas requiring 
continued attention. Where estimates, assumptions or 
limitations apply, these have been stated appropriately.
Frameworks and standards
This report conforms to the principles and guidelines of: 
•	 The Companies Act, 2013 (and the Rules made 
thereunder)
•	 Indian Accounting Standards
•	 Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015, includes Business Responsibility Sustainability 
Report (BRSR) and BRSR Core, 2023
•	 National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct 
(NGRBC)
•	 Secretarial Standards issued by the Institute of Company 
Secretaries of India
•	 International Financial Reporting Standards Foundation 
(IFRS)- S2
•	 United Nations Global Compact (UNGC) Ten Principles 
based on four pillars
•	 Global Reporting Initiative (GRI)
Wherever possible, we have aligned with emerging 
expectations on sustainability reporting and climate-related 
disclosures.
Data compilation methodology
The data in this integrated report is based on our best-
adopted practices and internationally recognised frameworks. 
We have computed carbon emissions utilising the GHG 
Protocol Standards for Scope 1, 2 and 3. We have also 
adopted guidance of World Business Council for Sustainability 
Development (WBCSD), Cement Sustainability Initiative (CSI) and 
European Cement Research Academy (ECRA), incorporating 
pertinent emission factors to quantify the emissions.
We have disclosed our non-financial metrics, demonstrating 
the change in our performance over the last few years. 
We reserve the right to change our internal guidelines 
regarding the inclusion of data in future integrated reports. 
Any modifications will be clearly communicated to our 
stakeholders.
Previous financial year’s (FY 2024-25) figures have 
been restated or recasted as J.K. Cement Limited has 
done amalgamation of Toshali Cements Pvt. Ltd. with effect 
from 1st April 2024.

This journey has been built on a clear strategy: expand

In FY 2025-26, we delivered on this 
promise. Our grey cement capacity 
grew from 24.34 MnTPA to 32.26 MnTPA 
through the commissioning of the

and Muddapur (1.0 MnTPA) along with 
acquisition of controlling stake in Saifco 
Cement (0.42 MnTPA). These additions 
were delivered on time and within 
budget, strengthening our presence 
across priority regions from Jammu and 
Kashmir to Eastern and Southern India.
Correspondingly, our grey cement volumes 
breached the 20 MT milestone during the 
year under review.

enhance market reach but to strengthen

Message from the Managing Director
Dear stakeholders,
As I reflect on FY 2025-26, I am filled with excitement 
about the progress we have made and the opportunities 
that lie ahead. Over the past five decades, JK Cement has 
demonstrated consistent, disciplined, and largely organic 
growth, a remarkable feat that speaks to the resilience of our 
business model, the commitment of our teams, and the trust 
of our stakeholders. This year, we have set new benchmark 
for operational and strategic performance while navigating a 
complex global operating environment with agility and resolve. 
What excites me is the pace and discipline of our execution. 
Over the last five years, we have more than doubled our grey 
cement capacity while evolving from a cement company into 
a comprehensive building materials player. This transformation 
positions us well for the next phase of our journey.
It was a defining year for JK Cement in every sense. Not 
merely in terms of financial and operational numbers, but 
in what those achievements represent: a business that is 
growing with greater confidence, expanding its scale with 
precision, and developing a clearer strategic vision for the 
years ahead. The confluence of disciplined execution and 
accelerated growth during this year captures both our journey 
and the philosophy with which we are building our future.
This has been a year when we have focused on the 
fundamentals: crossing critical capacity milestones, 
strengthening our balance sheet, deepening our regional 
presence, and building the operational and commercial 
infrastructure that will support the next phase of 
our expansion.
India's cement sector: A structural 
growth story
India's cement industry benefits from structural demand 
tailwinds that remain largely intact. The country's infrastructure 
creation aspirations, accelerating private capital expenditure, 
steady growth in housing, rural and affordable housing 
schemes, rapid urbanisation, and the broader long-term 
development priorities create a durable foundation for 
cement demand.
The Government's commitment to infrastructure 
development, coupled with rising private-sector investments 
in industrial capacity, data centres, and commercial real estate, 
underpins our conviction in the sector's enduring growth 
trajectory. Housing construction, whether in urban centres

and home ownership aspirations increase. This diversity of 
demand sources provides confidence that the cement sector 
will grow at a healthy pace over the foreseeable future.
We view this structural opportunity as something we must 
earn through superior execution, product quality and 
financial discipline. This reinforces our strategy of building 
capacity in the right regions and deepening penetration in 
chosen markets.
However, we must acknowledge a significant source of 
near-term uncertainty: the escalating geopolitical tensions 
in West Asia. Rising fuel costs, particularly imported pet 
coke and diesel and increasing cost of cement bags have 
started impacting cost. The Indian Rupee's depreciation has 
amplified these pressures. These directly affect our margins 
and competitiveness. We are navigating these through 
operational efficiencies, energy-mix optimisation, sourcing 
diversification, and calibrated pricing actions to neutralise 
the impact. However, if geopolitical tensions persist, the cost 
environment may face further headwinds. Despite these 
uncertainties, our conviction in India's long-term growth story 
remains unchanged.
Milestones achieved in FY 2025-26
After a journey of half a century, we have now entered our 
next phase of accelerated growth. During the year, we crossed 
two significant milestones in that journey that reflect years of 
sustained execution. Our grey cement capacity surpassed 
the 30 million tonnes per annum mark, and our grey cement 
volumes crossed 20 million tonnes for the first time in a full 
financial year. These achievements represent the outcome 
of consistent organic expansion, unshakeable management 
commitment, disciplined market-building, and execution 
excellence across our organisation.
We are now among India's top five cement companies by 
capacity. Our goal is not simply to be larger, but to grow in a 
manner that builds resilience, remains relevant to customer 
needs, and maintains the financial strength that enables us to 
invest meaningfully during economic cycles.
These achievements reflect a long-term approach to growth. 
We have invested ahead of demand, built market readiness 
before capacity stabilisation, and maintained a careful balance

Message from the Managing Director
Strategic expansion and regional 
presence
The year reinforced our strategy of strengthening presence 
in regions where we have built lasting market relevance, while 
selectively entering markets that enhance our long-term 
opportunity. Acquiring controlling stake in Saifco cement, 
expanded our footprint in Kashmir and northern markets, 
while our expansion across Central, Eastern, and Southern 
India has improved our ability to serve key demand corridors 
with greater speed and responsiveness.
Our immediate capacity roadmap reflects this disciplined 
regional approach. New projects across Rajasthan and 
Northern India, along with subsequent phases at Muddapur 
and Panna, are designed to deepen our market position in 
regions where we have strategic presence. This focused 
strategy reduces execution risk, improves capital efficiency, 
and builds sustainable competitive advantages in 
chosen markets.
Our value-added products portfolio is gaining strategic 
traction. The upcoming Nathdwara wall putty plant will 
improve supply efficiency and category depth, while our 
growing paints business, supported by a dedicated R&D 
facility, is opening new categories and customer segments. 
Our initial foray into ready-mix concrete through an asset-light 
model positions us to deepen our building-materials relevance 
and participate more directly in evolving construction 
practices. In the coming years, we aspire to scale this to 
around 100 RMC plants.
Internationally, our UAE operations are extending beyond white 
cement into dry-mix solutions and construction chemicals, 
reinforcing our overseas building materials strategy. 
This products-to-solutions movement enables deeper 
customer engagement, gives our channel partners a wider 
and more valuable basket and builds resilience across multiple 
product categories.
Resource security 
Resource security remains a critical pillar of our long‑term 
growth strategy. During the year, we obtained the LOIs of 
four limestone blocks across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan 
and Andhra Pradesh to support existing reserves and 
future growth. As part of our broader fuel security and cost 
optimisation agenda, we also initiated the development 
of captive coal assets. Progress is underway towards 
operationalising the Mahan and West of Shahdol coal blocks, 
which will enhance supply security, reduce input cost volatility 
and strengthen our long-term energy resilience.

People, safety, and workplace culture
Our people remain at the heart of our success. During 
FY 2025-26, we successfully transitioned project teams 
into operating roles while strengthening a comprehensive 
safety culture across all operations.
Safety has evolved from compliance-led systems to 
embedded behavioural initiatives. Our Roko-Toko-Sudhar 
Karo programme empowers employees to identify and 
correct unsafe actions in real time, fostering accountability. 
Chai Pe Charcha creates informal forums for open safety 
conversations and peer engagement.
Beyond these behavioural initiatives, we have 
implemented Project YATRA with competency building, 
zone ownership concepts, and monthly Safety Gate 
meetings celebrating safe practices. Initiatives span 
road and logistics safety through JRM protocols, fire 
safety audits, and process safety strengthening. Safety 
automation, including face recognition access systems, 
enhances operational security.
At our Jaisalmer greenfield project, we have engaged 
DSS as safety consultants. We are implementing 
specialised programmes address height-specific risks 
through acrophobia testing and height rescue training, 
with robust emergency preparedness protocols.
This integrated approach of combining behavioural 
initiatives, technology, training, and culture has created 
a workforce genuinely accountable for safe operations.
Community engagement and  
shared value
Our responsibility extends beyond our plants and 
operations to the communities in which we operate. 
During the year, our CSR initiatives continued to create 
meaningful impact across education, healthcare, 
livelihoods, water access and rural infrastructure. 
Education remains a key area of focus, with sustained 
investments in strengthening learning infrastructure and 
expanding access to quality education in communities 
around our manufacturing locations. Today, every one 
of our manufacturing units is associated with a school, 
reflecting our long-term commitment to nurturing future 
generations. These initiatives are not purely philanthropic; 
they reflect our belief that sustainable business success 
requires healthy, prosperous communities. We have 
also set up vocational training institutes at most of our 
integrated cement manufacturing plants.
Looking ahead
As we look ahead, our strategic priorities are clear: sustain 
our position among India's top five cement companies, 
deepen our presence in regions of strategic choice, 
advance our long-term capacity roadmap of 50+ MnTPA, 
continue strengthening our building-materials portfolio, 
and maintain the financial discipline that has served 
us well.
The external environment will remain dynamic. However, 
we are well-prepared to navigate these challenges on 
the strength of our execution capabilities, expanded 
financial capacity, diversified portfolio, and the trust of our 
stakeholders.
I thank our shareholders, customers, dealers, employees, 
suppliers, logistics partners, communities, regulators, 
and all stakeholders for their continued trust and 
support. We remain committed to building JK Cement 
with the same values that have guided us for more than 
five decades: discipline, responsibility, resilience, and 
a commitment to creating enduring value for all our 
stakeholders.
Best regards,

Green power mix
Operational excellence and 
cost discipline
Cost and productivity remain fundamental priorities. 
Fuel volatility, logistics trends, packaging inflation, and 
geopolitical developments required relentless attention. 
We responded through energy-mix optimisation, 
greater green power usage, alternative fuels strategies 
and rigorous cost discipline. At the plant level, capacity 
debottlenecking, waste heat recovery systems, energy 
efficiency initiatives and digital process intelligence 
reduced per tonne cash costs. 
Progressive capacity roadmap
Beyond FY 2025-26, we have a clear medium-term 
capacity expansion agenda. At Jaisalmer, an integrated 
project comprising 4 MnTPA of clinker capacity and 
3 MnTPA of cement capacity is progressing well, with 
civil construction and equipment erection advancing on 
schedule. This project will significantly strengthen our 
presence in North India markets.
Planned split grinding units in Rajasthan and Punjab will 
provide shorter-distance market access to Northern 
India, improving our competitive position and logistics 
economics. The Nathdwara wall putty plant is progressing 
as scheduled, enabling us to serve dealers meaningfully.
As these new capacities come onstream and stabilise, 
our focus will remain on improving fixed-cost absorption 
through volume growth, strengthening service reliability 
and responsiveness, and ensuring that recently 
commissioned assets deliver the operating leverage they 
are designed for. We will continue the disciplined, phased 
approach that has characterised our expansion: building 
ahead of demand, establishing market position before 
stabilisation, and transitioning operational teams from 
project roles into steady-state operating functions.
Embedding sustainability into 
operations
For JK Cement, sustainability is embedded into how we 
operate our plants and manage our supply chains. During 
the year, our green power mix reached 51.8%, reported 
thermal substitution rate of 11.97% and water positivity 
of 4.9x. We continue to scale waste heat recovery, 
renewable energy, and water conservation initiatives. 
Importantly, sustainability is part of how we run plants 
better, reduce risk, improve efficiency, and prepare for a 
more carbon‑conscious future where energy costs and 
regulations will only increase. We are proud to state that all 
our integrated plants run WHRS system. 
Expanding value-added products range
Our value-added products portfolio has gained significant 
traction during the year. White cement and wall putty 
continued their contribution to overall profitability, while 
construction chemicals, tile adhesives, grouts, and paints 
expanded our relevance across the complete building 
lifecycle. For individual home builders and applicators, 
our mission is to provide the right cement and the right 
auxiliary product for the right application.
As our value-added products basket strengthens, we 
become a more valuable partner to our customers and 
channel partners. Builders prefer a single source for 
multiple products, improving our relevance and share of 
wallet. Retailers can stock a broader range of JK products, 
increasing basket size and profitability. End users benefit 
from integrated solutions that simplify their purchasing 
decisions and improve construction quality.
Enhancing brand visibility 
During the year, JK Cement significantly strengthened 
brand salience through strategic partnerships and 
influencer engagement. We signed Bollywood actor 
Akshay Kumar as brand ambassador for the JK Maxx 
premium range, enhancing market visibility and recall. 
Additionally, we deepened our sports engagement 
through association with Lucknow Super Giants (LSG). 
These brand investments, coupled with targeted digital 
activations and wider market campaigns, reinforced JK 
Cement's positioning as a premium, aspirational brand 
while strengthening customer and dealer engagement 
across its expanding building-materials portfolio.
The road ahead is clear
As we look ahead to FY 2026-27 and beyond, our 
priorities are clear: stabilise the capacity added during 
this year, drive utilisation improvements, deepen market 
reach in chosen regions, continue strengthening our 
value-added products portfolio, sustain the journey on 
premiumisation, scale digital enablement and data-driven 
decision-making, embed safety even more deeply into our 
culture, and accelerate our sustainability journey across all 
dimensions of our operations.
We remain agile in a competitive market, responsive to 
customer needs and market dynamics, and disciplined 
in our execution. This combination of agility and discipline 
has brought us this far and it will continue to guide us.
I thank our employees, channel partners, customers, 
suppliers, logistics partners, and all our stakeholders for 
their trust and support. Together, we are unlocking JK 
Cement's next phase of growth and building a company 
that is larger, stronger, more responsible, and more 
valuable for all who have invested in our journey.
Sincerely,
Madhavkrishna Singhania

India’s cement industry is undergoing a structural growth 
phase, supported by sustained infrastructure investments 
by the Government of India and robust demand from the real 
estate sector, resulting in annual industry growth of 7%.
Despite being the world’s second-largest cement market, 
India’s per capita cement consumption continues to remain 
significantly below global averages, underscoring substantial 
long-term growth potential. During the year, demand 
momentum remained particularly strong across North, Central 
and Eastern India, driven by infrastructure execution and 
housing activity. Southern and Western regions, meanwhile, 
witnessed relatively stable demand trends. Overall, the 
industry maintained a steady growth trajectory, reflecting the 
resilience of underlying demand fundamentals.
The pricing environment in India’s cement sector in 
FY 2025-26 showed gradual recovery from prior year 
volatility, supported by ~5% demand. Average prices rose year 
on year in select periods, though trends varied across regions 
and seasons.
Pricing remained regionally uneven: Southern and Eastern 
markets saw stronger early improvements, while Northern 
and Central regions faced intermittent pressure due to supply 
additions and competition. Seasonal factors, especially the 
monsoon, temporarily impacted dispatches and pricing. 
Capacity additions influenced utilisation, but overall utilisation 
reflected steady demand absorption on an expanded base, 
with clinker utilisation generally higher than grinding levels.
PRICING AND MARKET DISCIPLINE
The input cost environment for India’s cement sector in 
FY 2025-26 showed a mixed trend. Energy prices were 
relatively stable during parts of the year but rose towards 
year‑end due to West Asia-linked crude and imported fuel 
pressures, keeping energy‑cost management, fuel‑mix 
flexibility and sourcing discipline central.
Imported fuels such as coal and pet coke remained below 
earlier peak levels for part of the year, but rising year‑end 
costs limited relief, reinforcing the focus on domestic sourcing, 
alternative fuels and disciplined planning.
Freight and logistics costs remained variable due to lead 
distances, modal mix and regional imbalances, although 
capacity additions closer to demand centres and improved 
clinker logistics helped moderate costs in some regions. 
Industry capacity utilisation remained ~74%, reflecting steady 
demand absorption, with clinker utilisation generally higher 
than grinding levels due to inter‑regional balancing.

Power-load management - Mangrol

Infinite Uptime sensors were installed at Nimbahera,

Predicting cement strength for proactive

We developed a cement strength prediction tool

Waste Utilisation
RDF dust ash as replacement of fly ash in 
PPC production
Research collaboration: In-house
We initiated a waste utilisation project to use RDF dust ash as 
a fly ash replacement in PPC. RDF dust from trommel/ballistic 
separators is heated at 950°C and converted into cementitious 
ash. The pathway can utilise 10-15 TPD RDF sieving dust, 
reduce fly ash use by ~50% and potentially up to 100% under 
trial, while lowering procurement, transport, handling, disposal 
and storage costs.
Process Efficiency
Efficient use of grinding aids to reduce 
electrical energy
Research collaboration: In-house
Trials are underway across various grinding units using 
different grinding-aid sources to improve grinding efficiency 
and reduce electrical energy consumption. The initiative 
focuses on improving particle dispersion, reducing 
agglomeration, increasing mill throughput and lowering 
specific power consumption per tonne of cement. Once 
validated across sources and locations, the project can 
support process efficiency and energy-cost optimisation.
New Product
Development and product optimisation for 
specific application
Research collaboration: In-house
During the year, we optimised OPC-53 for specialised precast, 
RMC and infrastructure applications, addressing customer 
needs for faster deployment, better workability, lighter 
colour, durability and consistency. Further, We developed 
OPC-53 Fast Set for precast and OPC-53 Strong Set for 
RMCs/infrastructure, supporting stronger performance in 
high-end construction segments.
Product/Standards Support
Portland limestone cement development
Research collaboration: In-house
During FY 2025-26, the Portland Limestone Cement (PLC) 
initiative progressed from formulation development to the 
completion of technical evaluation. The study validated the 
integration of 12% limestone in PLC, supporting reduced 
clinker intensity without compromising cement performance. 
The project strengthens our preparedness for the future 
adoption of lower-clinker cement products, subject to the 
issuance of the relevant BIS standard and market acceptance.
Product/Standards Support
Portland composite cement development
Research collaboration: In-house
Our Portland Composite Cement (PCC) study evaluated 
the use of finely ground limestone as a partial replacement 
for fly ash. Completed during the year, the study identified 
optimal performance when limestone replaced fly ash in the 
range of 5% to 10%, while maintaining clinker and gypsum 
content at 65%. The findings were shared with the Cement 
Manufacturers’ Association to contribute to industry-wide 
discussions on lower-clinker cement formulations.
Plant Support
Root-cause analysis for cement lumps and 
clinker disintegration
Research collaboration: In-house
During the year, two plant-support studies enhanced root-
cause analysis and troubleshooting capabilities. In the case of 
cement lump formation, standard operating procedures were 
developed following an assessment of moisture levels, storage 
conditions, clinker characteristics, gypsum dehydration, alkali 
content and silo-related factors. The study concluded that 
lump formation was marginal and primarily associated with 
bag damage. For clinker disintegration, the analysis identified 
poor clinkerisation, incomplete conversion of C2S to C3S, the 
presence of γ-C2S and unstable clinker nodules as the key 
factors contributing to fine generation during transportation.
AFR Process Support
Adsorbent-based chloride removal from 
alternative fuels and raw materials
Collaboration: Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur
We continued work on an adsorbent-based process to 
remove chlorides from alternative fuels and raw materials. 
This initiative supports higher AFR utilisation by addressing 
operational issues such as corrosion, coating build-up, process 
instability and clinker-quality concerns. The IIT Kanpur study 
recommended BiO2-HNO3 and CaO-NaAlO2 systems as 
adsorbents for chloride removal. The next stage will involve 
further validation of process applicability, operational feasibility 
and performance under plant-relevant conditions.

A sustainability issue is material if 
it significantly impacts society or 
the environment and influences 
a company’s value drivers, 
competitiveness and long-term 
value creation. Material ESG issues 
affect operations, cash flows, 
compliance and capital access, 
while shaping reputation and 
stakeholder relationships, often 
translating external impacts into 
internal financial outcomes.
Materiality assessment
Our approach to materiality
We initiated our first comprehensive materiality 
assessment in FY 2020-21, followed by an impact 
assessment in FY 2024-25, and a double materiality 
assessment in FY 2025-26 to identify financial and 
impact priorities. Inputs from internal and external 
stakeholders were incorporated, with outcomes 
embedded into ERM and approved by top leadership.
Our materiality assessment process
The assessment methodology was designed to comply with 
CSRD standards while integrating JK Cement’s existing risk 
universe and insights from previous materiality assessments. 
This approach ensured consistency in evaluating financial 
risks and broadened the scope to include a comprehensive 
analysis of sustainability-related impacts and opportunities.
Scope and contextualise
We define our boundaries and operating context 
by reviewing legal and financial structures to 
identify CSRD‑covered entities. We also map our 
value chain to understand stakeholders and our 
operating environment.
Identify ESG topics
We identify a broad set of ESG issues by analysing 
global standards, sector trends and internal 
strategies, supported by peer benchmarking and 
risk databases.
Build the longlist
We consolidate and map issues to ESRS 
sub‑topics, creating a structured longlist. 
We engage stakeholders to assess relevance, 
value chain positioning and potential impacts.
Assess IROs
We identify impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) 
using dual materiality, evaluating environmental/
social outcomes and financial implications, to guide 
action and value creation.
Score and engage
We score each IRO using ESRS criteria and validate 
through stakeholder consultations across five 
groups to ensure balanced perspectives.
Set thresholds
We apply defined thresholds for each stakeholder 
group to finalise material topics, while allowing 
strategic elevation where required five groups to 
ensure balanced perspectives.
Finalise and map
We refine the final list and map it on a materiality 
matrix, showcasing priorities across impact and 
financial dimensions.

Sustainability governance structure
JK Cement has set up a strong governance structure to foster 
sustainable operations. The CSR and Sustainability Committee 
oversees the workings of the Sustainability Steering 
Committee. This committee comprises of the Joint Managing 
Director, C-suite executives and the Head of Sustainability.
CSR and Sustainability Committee
The Committee’s primary role is to support our Board in 
fulfilling its sustainability commitments by formulating 
and overseeing the implementation of policies related to 
sustainable operations. It also promotes strong corporate 
governance practices and recommends appropriate 
corrective measures where necessary.
Sustainability Steering Committee
The Committee provides recommendations to the CSR and 
Sustainability Committee, which submits quarterly updates 
to our Board. Our Board, in turn, sets the key objectives and 
guides management in achieving sustainability goals within 
the established framework.
Corporate Sustainability Council
The Sustainability Council, comprising plant and functional 
heads, leads the implementation of sustainability initiatives 
across our facilities. It drives awareness, ensures alignment 
with global best practices, supports audits and facilitates 
reporting and stakeholder disclosures. The Council also 
participates in sustainability awards and ratings. Plant‑level 
Sustainability Champions work closely with the Council, 
providing insights to the Sustainability Steering Committee 
to strengthen our Company’s overall environmental and 
social performance.
Climate governance and strategy
Our Company maintains a strong climate governance 
framework that integrates climate‑related risks and 
opportunities into its core business strategy. Oversight 
rests with our Board of Directors, supported by the CSR 
and Sustainability Committee, which meets quarterly to 
review climate performance and progress. Our Board 
defines our climate vision, approves emission reduction 
targets and monitors outcomes, while senior management 
drives effective execution.
To strengthen implementation, an executive‑level 
Committee, chaired by the Joint Managing Director 
and CEO, oversees strategic execution and monitors 
performance against defined sustainability metrics. 
Climate matters are a standing agenda item at every 
quarterly Board meeting, reinforcing accountability at the 
highest level.
The Head of Manufacturing and Sustainability leads the 
operational response, driving on‑ground climate initiatives 
across all locations.
Aligned with our Company’s ESG priorities, the Nomination 
and Remuneration Committee (NRC) has linked the 
variable pay of the Joint MD and CEO, business heads 
and manufacturing heads to ESG performance, based on 
predefined KPIs approved by our Board.
Climate change-related awards and 
incentives
We have integrated sustainability into our core operations, 
fostering a culture of environmental responsibility across 
all levels of the organisation. To strengthen participation, 
we have introduced targeted incentives that encourage 
employees to contribute to climate‑risk management 
and resource‑efficient practices. By linking individual 
performance with climate objectives and promoting 
innovation in water and energy conservation, waste heat 
recovery and circular economy initiatives, we continue 
to advance our sustainability agenda. To drive proactive 
climate action and resource optimisation, JK Cement 
aligns employee performance with the Company's 
sustainability targets. Climate objectives and risk mitigation 
goals—managed via the proactive Kaizen approach—are 
integrated directly into annual Key Performance Indicators 
(KPIs).
To foster continuous grassroots innovation, the company 
actively incentivises employees through targeted 
recognition programmes for optimising water & energy 
consumption, improving production efficiency, and 
circular economy advancements, like improving Thermal

management, and low-grade limestone consumption.

Our approach to shareholder value creation is rooted in disciplined growth, earnings resilience, prudent financial management

profitability while continuing to invest in our growth pipeline. Reflecting the strength of our financial performance and confidence 
in future cash flows, the Board recommended a final dividend of I 20 per equity share, up 33.3% over the previous year.

leadership and achieving industry-benchmark EBITDA per tonne is expected to strengthen profitability and drive long-term 
shareholder value.

that guides responsible and transparent tax conduct

stakeholder confidence.

Our capital deployment during FY 2025-26 focused on 
strengthening manufacturing capacity, market access, 
value-added products and long-term competitiveness.

was completed with approximately 10% savings against 
the planned project cost of I 2,850 Crores, reflecting 
strong project governance and capital efficiency.

comprised I 914 Crores for the greenfield expansion in 
North, whereas I 100 Crores have been spent on the 
6 Lakhs TPA wall putty facility at Nathdwara.

and I 2,000-2,500 Crores in FY 2027-28, including 
sustenance and coal block-related investments, will result 
in additional capacity, coal availability at competitive 
cost and investment in renewable power. This will help in 
increasing earning of the company.

and under execution enhance operating leverage potential

Governance and management systems
At JK Cement, the health, safety and well-being of our 
people remain a core priority. Our Occupational Health and 
Safety (OHS) Policy, overseen by the Board of Directors, 
applies across all manufacturing operations, grinding 
units and corporate offices, covering 100% of permanent 
employees, contractors and third-party workers under our 
supervision. We comply with applicable national regulations, 
statutory requirements and international standards, including 
ISO 45001:2018.
Our OHS framework promotes active worker participation 
through site-level Safety Committees, safety circles and 
hazard-identification forums. We continuously strengthen 
our systems through benchmarking, structured annual 
safety action plans and risk-based corrective and preventive 
measures. To advance our Zero Harm ambition, we track key 
leading and lagging indicators, including LTIFR, near-miss 
reporting and safety training hours, while maintaining time-
bound improvement targets.

Key projects and technological interventions
	
	
Carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) 
As part of our steadfast commitment to achieving Net 
Zero by 2070, we have transitioned into a critical phase 
of technological intervention through carbon capture 
and utilisation (CCU). Recognising that process-related 
emissions are the most ‘hard-to-abate’ in cement 
manufacturing, we have spearheaded a flagship 2 TPD 
(tonnes per day) CCU pilot project in collaboration with 
the National Council for Cement and Building Materials 
(NCCBM) and IIT Roorkee. Unlike conventional post-
combustion capture, our innovative approach focuses 
on oxygen-based calcination. 
This process involves utilising oxygen-enriched air in 
the calciner to increase the concentration of CO2 in 
the flue gas. This efficiently isolates the CO2 stream, 
which is then diverted for high-value utilisation rather 
than storage. The captured CO2 is integrated into 
the production of lightweight concrete products and 
olefins, effectively locking the carbon into the built 
environment and creating a circular value chain.
Steel slag reborn 
This initiative tackles the hard-to-abate carbon 
footprints of both steelmaking and cement production 
simultaneously. JK Cement and Tata Steel have 
formed a strategic industrial alliance under the global 
LeadIT initiative to drive circular economy solutions. 
The partnership centers on a high-profile collaborative 
project with Sweden's Cemvision and IIT-ISM Dhanbad 
to commercially process low-grade steel waste, 
specifically Basic Oxygen Furnace (BOF) slag, which 
is traditionally difficult to recycle. By using advanced 
thermal modification, they reclaim valuable residual 
metals for Tata Steel while transforming the remaining 
slag into a highly reactive raw material for JK Cement. 
This cross-industry symbiosis allows JK Cement 
to drastically lower its clinker-to-cement ratio and 
process emissions, while simultaneously shrinking 
Tata Steel's industrial waste footprint.
Air emissions
Air emissions management remains a key focus area within 
our environmental agenda. As a cement manufacturer, our 
operations emit sulphur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx) 
and particulate matter (PM), which are controlled through 
electrostatic precipitators (ESPs), bag houses and bag filters 
installed across our manufacturing facilities. Continuous 
monitoring systems has been installed for real-time monitoring 
of stack emissions and ambient air quality. Various process 
optimisation and technology upgrades also support in 
compliance with the prescribed regulatory standards. 
We comply with conditions stipulated in various regulatory 
permissions, such as Environment Clearance (EC), Consent to 
Establish (CTE), Consent to Operate (CTO), etc, across all our 
sites. During the reporting year, ozone-depleting substance 
(ODS) emissions remained minimal at 0.03 MT of CFC-11 
equivalent. Further, we have third-party monitoring through 
NABL-accredited labs.

BIODIVERSITY
Biodiversity conservation is integral to our approach to responsible growth and environmental stewardship. Guided by our 
Biodiversity Policy, we implement site-specific action plans developed in collaboration with local stakeholders and expert teams. 
Our approach aligns with the CII-India Business & Biodiversity Initiative (IBBI) and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity 
Framework. We assess projects using the mitigation hierarchy of avoid, minimise, restore and offset to manage biodiversity 
impacts effectively. We maintain a strict prohibition on involvement in the trade of CITES-listed species and work to prevent 
adverse impacts on threatened flora and fauna. Ecosystem restoration, native species plantation and the development of 
self-sustaining green corridors remain key focus areas.
Operational footprint and site sensitivity
We manage a significant land area ~8,400 hectares across 
13 operational sites, including manufacturing cement plants, 
grinding units and mines. We recognise that our presence 
in these landscapes carries a responsibility to monitor 
and mitigate our ‘inside-out’ impacts. While none of our 
mentioned operations are located within notified protected 
areas or high-biodiversity value zones, we maintain a policy 
of heightened vigilance for sites near sensitive ecosystems. 
Biodiversity risk assessment
Before any project expansion or initiation, we conduct 
comprehensive environmental impact assessments (EIAs) 
that analyse biodiversity within a 10-kilometre radius of 
project boundaries. These studies result in preparation 
of site-specific wildlife management plans (WMPs) in 
consultation with local authorities with clear, time-bound 
conservation targets.
Our Panna integrated plant is located ~13 km from the 
Panna Tiger Reserve, this site is a priority location for 
our management teams, from biodiversity conservation 
perspective. In addition to implementation of site-specific 
wildlife conservation plan, we have also initiated biodiversity 
risk assessment at this location in line with TNFD LEAP 
Approach. The results of this study indicate no negative 
impact of our operations on the ecosystem.
Biodiversity assessment: The LEAP 
approach
During FY 2025-26, we initiated assessing the dependency- 
and impact- related biodiversity risk covering our own 
operations and adjacent areas covering an aerial radius 
of 10 km. We have initiated a location-specific approach 
in Nimbahera, Mangrol and Panna. This methodology is 
aligned with TNFD’s LEAP approach. The methodology 
allows us to systematically analyse its dependencies and 
impacts on natural resources, evaluate potential risks and 
identify opportunities for positive contributions. By applying 
the LEAP approach, the units integrate nature-related 
considerations into operational and strategic planning, 
ensuring that sustainability and ecological resilience remain 
central to decision-making. To manage our environmental 
dependencies, we have adopted the TNFD-aligned LEAP 
methodology, integrating nature-related risks directly into 
our corporate strategy.
Locate (geographic interface)
We map our operational footprint against local 
ecosystems to establish detailed biodiversity 
baselines. This stage identifies proximity to 
protected areas (PAs), key biodiversity areas (KBAs) 
and other sites of high conservation importance to 
ensure geographic sensitivity.
2
Evaluate (dependencies and Impacts)
We apply a dual ‘inside-out’ and ‘outside-in’ 
assessment. We evaluate how much our operations 
depend on ecosystem services (e.g. water and 
climate regulation) and the corresponding impact 
our activities have on natural capital. This materiality 
matrix prioritises the most critical ecosystem 
services for sustainable management.
3
Assess (risks and opportunities) 
Using a dependency-impact matrix, we classify 
nature-related risks from very high to low. This 
identifies physical, regulatory and reputational 
threats while uncovering opportunities in 
biodiversity stewardship and nature-positive 
practices. These findings are integrated into 
our multi-disciplinary, organisation-wide risk 
management processes.
4
Prepare (response and integration) 
We develop site-specific biodiversity management 
plans (BMP). Mitigation follows a strict hierarchy: 
avoid, minimise, restore and offset for any residual 
impacts. This ensures that nature-positive 
outcomes are embedded in our long-term financial 
and operational planning.
To systematically identify and manage nature-related 
dependencies, impacts, risks, and opportunities (DIRO), 
we utilise the TNFD's LEAP framework alongside global 
tools like the WRI Ecosystem Services Review and the WWF 
Biodiversity Risk Filter.
Biodiversity, and nature-related risks & opportunities 
Risks
Dependency-related risks (outside-in)
Using the ENCORE tool, we identified that our manufacturing 
and mining operations have high to very high dependencies 
on specific ecosystem services. If these ecosystems degrade, 
it directly threatens operational continuity. Key dependencies 
include:
•	 Water supply for operations and domestic use
•	 Water purification and flow regulation services
•	 Flood and storm mitigation services
•	 Global climate regulation and rainfall pattern regulation
Impact-related and ecological risks  
(inside-out)
We also evaluate the pressures our operations exert on the 
environment, which can lead to ecological degradation and 
subsequent business risks. Key impacts include:
•	 Resource depletion and emissions: Significant impact 
risks arise from the area and volume of freshwater use, 
land-use alteration and emissions of GHG and non-GHG 
air pollutants.
•	 Socio-environmental and reputational risks: Depleting 
shared resources (like groundwater) or creating dust 
and noise pollution can limit a local community's access 
to vital resources. This can spark socio-environmental 
conflicts, protests and the ultimate loss of our ‘social 
license to operate’. Furthermore, failure to meet ESG goals 
can result in regulatory setbacks and damage to brand 
reputation.
•	 Physical and transition risks: We face acute physical 
risks (floods and droughts) and chronic risks (water 
stress and temperature variations) that can damage 
assets or disrupt supply chains. Transition risks include 
emerging climate regulations (like carbon pricing), 
technological developments and market shifts toward 
greener products.
Opportunities
We strategically transform environmental challenges into 
business opportunities to build long-term resilience:
Resource efficiency and circular economy
By reducing our reliance on virgin natural resources (like 
high-grade limestone), we minimise our ecological footprint. 
We achieve this by lowering our clinker-to-cement ratio and 
co-processing industrial, agricultural and municipal waste as 
alternative fuel and raw materials (AFR).
Water conservation and replenishment
Operating in dry regions provides the opportunity to 
implement highly efficient closed-loop water systems. 
Through rainwater harvesting, zero-liquid discharge systems 
and mine water treatment, we have achieved a 4.9x water 
positivity rate and target 5x by 2030.
Energy transition
Transitioning to low-carbon energy reduces dependence on 
external power grids and mitigates transition risks. We are 
aggressively expanding our WHRS and renewable energy mix, 
targeting a 75% green power share by 2030.
Access to new markets
By doing afforestation beyond our boundaries, we are 
positioning ourselves to benefit from emerging green credits 
markets which could provide additional revenue streams.
Ecosystem restoration and net gain
Investing in nature-based solutions, such as converting 
exhausted mine pits into vital water reservoirs for migratory 
birds and developing the 50-hectare Biodiversity Park in 
Nimbahera, helping us offset carbon emissions and secure 
community goodwill.

SUSTAINABLE PRODUCTS
We are advancing a portfolio of high-performance construction materials that combine durability, reliability and environmental 
responsibility. Our product development approach integrates low-carbon design, material efficiency and lifecycle thinking to 
align with evolving green building standards and customer expectations. We are committed to enhancing the environmental and 
health transparency of our products. 
To meet evolving green building standards and 
customer expectations: 
•	 Our cement products, JK Super PPC, JK Super 
PSC and JK Super Strong PPC are GreenPro-
certified 
•	 Our product brochures include health and 
environmental declarations, ensuring responsible 
communication regarding material composition, 
potential health hazards and environmental 
attributes
The distinguishing features of our construction 
products are: 
•	 Locally extracted or recovered materials from the 
mines surrounding our plants 
•	 Low embodied carbon materials such as Portland 
Slag Cement and Portland Pozzolana Cement by 
recycling fly ash, slag as well as AFR 
•	 VOC from the product manufacturing is negligible 
•	 All our products disclose potential health hazards 
•	 Commitment to safe and eco-friendly materials 
As part of our alignment with the Red List of prohibited 
materials published by the International Living Future Institute, 
we ensure that none of the following harmful substances 
like mercury, cadmium, lead, CFCs, PVC, halogenated flame 
retardants, formaldehyde (added), or similar toxic materials 
are used in our manufacturing processes. This reflects our 
commitment to providing safe products for people and the 
planet. We continuously train our R&D and production teams 
on sustainable product innovation. Our research is focused on 
developing low-carbon cements and alternative binders that 
meet the performance requirements of modern infrastructure 
while reducing environmental impact.
Life cycle assessment
We apply science-based tools to quantify and reduce the 
environmental footprint of our products across their entire life 
cycle. A comprehensive life cycle assessment (LCA) has been 
undertaken in accordance with ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 
standards using recognised modelling software, enabling a 
structured evaluation of impacts from raw material extraction 
to final dispatch.
This assessment strengthens our ability to:
•	 Benchmark product performance across key 
environmental indicators
•	 Support credible environmental product declarations 
(EPDs) and health product declarations
•	 Identify emission and resource ‘hotspots’ for targeted 
process optimisation
•	 Enhance regulatory preparedness and align with green 
procurement and sustainability index requirements
Methodology
We conducted Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) studies across 
our major operational boundaries, including Nimbahera, 
Mangrol and Muddapur plants, covering multiple cement 
variants. Using a cradle-to-gate approach, the assessment 
evaluated environmental impacts from raw material extraction 
and transportation through manufacturing and emissions, up 
to the factory gate, with one tonne of cement as the functional 
unit. Based on the ReCiPe LCIA methodology, the study 
assessed impacts across categories including GHG emissions, 
ozone depletion, particulate matter formation, acidification, 
eutrophication, land use and human health. The assessment 
confirmed that blended cements such as PPC, PSC and 
composite cement have significantly lower environmental 
impacts than OPC, supporting our low-carbon product 
strategy and decarbonisation roadmap while strengthening 
data-driven environmental decision-making.

Climate change has emerged as one of the most pressing global 
challenges, drawing heightened attention from investors, regulators, 
customers and civil society. Stakeholders increasingly expect 
organisations to demonstrate climate resilience, transparency and 
accountability in how they manage the evolving risks posed by a 
warming planet. As a result, climate risk assessment is no longer just 
a sustainable consideration, it is a strategic imperative. 
OUR APPROACH TO 
CLIMATE RISK
Climate risk assessment 
To have a strategic response to mitigate the impact of climate 
change induced risks, we have undertaken a comprehensive 
climate risk assessment for our operations across India. 
Based on the outcome of the assessments, risk mitigation 
recommendations and measures were designed and 
inculcated in our overall business strategy to minimise the 
negative impacts of climate change induced risks.
In this context, Climate Change Risk assessment (CCRA) 
serves as a foundational step for the company, not only 
towards identification and mitigation of climate-related 
risks but also to seize emerging opportunities. It involves 
a systematic evaluation of both climate change induced, 
physical and transition risks linked to climate change, enabling 
organisations to build long-term resilience and align with global 
disclosure frameworks such as the Task Force on Climate-
related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations and 
IFRS S2 Standard.
Relevance to our business
As the effects of climate change become more evident, 
we face increasing risks such as revenue losses from supply 
chain disruptions and decreased productivity, infrastructural 
damage from extreme weather events, and higher operational 
costs due to stricter environmental regulations. Additionally, 
shifts in market dynamics can impact raw material availability 
and consumer preferences, while reputational risks arise if we 
are perceived as environmentally irresponsible. Implementing 
proactive climate strategies is crucial for JK Cement to 
mitigate these impacts and ensure sustainable growth. 
Conducting a CCRA allows us to proactively manage the 
identified potential risks, along with opportunities and build 
climate resilience across our operations and value chain.
Scenario analysis
At JK Cement, climate scenario analysis has been undertaken 
for distinct timeframes to assess potential implications of 
climate change under various global warming trajectories 
(e.g. 1.5°C, 2°C and 4°C scenarios). These scenarios 
are aligned with frameworks provided by the IPCC 
(Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) and the IEA 
(International Energy Agency). All the sites of our operations at 
Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Rajasthan and Bihar were evaluated against identified climate 
change induced hazards for these scenarios. For assessing 
the climate change induced hazards, we have considered the 
latest scenarios as outlined by the Intergovernmental Panel on 
Climate Change’s (IPCC) AR6 (Sixth Assessment Report) i.e. 
Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) scenarios for our operations 
spread across seven states.
SSP2 scenario (middle of the road)
SSP2 offers a moderate pathway of future socioeconomic 
development and associated emissions.
SSP5 scenario (fossil fuel development)
SSP5 represents a higher emissions scenario, allowing us to 
understand the potential range of physical impacts.
Each climate change scenario is mapped for the projected 
distinct timeframes which are in accordance with four 
timeframes as outlined by The World Bank Group.
•	 2020-2039
•	 2040-2059
•	 2060-2079
•	 2080-2099
Similarly, for transition risk assessment, we have considered 
the following scenarios to assess the potential risks against the 
three-timeframes.
IEA NZE 2050 scenario
NZE 2050 outlines a pathway for the sectors to globally 
achieve net zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.
B2DC scenario
B2DC refers to global efforts to limit the increase in average 
global temperatures to below 2°C above pre-industrial levels.
Each of the scenarios were assessed against the three defined 
timeframes as outlined by the TCFD framework,
•	 2025-2029
•	 2030-2039
•	 2040-2070

Identification of climate change-related risks
Physical risk
We, at JK Cement, have conducted a comprehensive analysis of climate change that induced hazards for the selected sites/
operations (within the risk assessment boundary) under two selected SSP scenarios as highlighted above. The table below 
highlights key potential climate change induced hazards identified for our operations across India and their potential business 
implications.
Flood/extreme 
rainfall
Hazard pattern: 
Acute 
Disruption in supply chain
Acute flooding can significantly disrupt the surface transportation of raw materials used in cement 
manufacturing such as limestone, gypsum and coal, leading to potential production delays. Additionally, 
it might further impact on the distribution of the finished product, due to disrupted access to transportation 
and further increased logistics cost.
Operational disruptions
Cement manufacturing plants in flood-prone areas are highly susceptible to significant physical damage from 
waterlogging, which can impact functioning of machinery like crushers, stackers and reclaimers, segregation 
machinery used in raw material handling, among others. Flooding/extreme rainfall can also lead to significant 
water infiltration in industrial facilities, resulting in operational delays, ground-level equipment damage, 
material damage and damage to electrical rooms. Additionally, flooding/extreme rainfall can cause regional 
power outages, resulting in production delays/disruptions.
Economic impact
The cumulative effects of these disruptions, supply chain interruptions, facility damage, operational halts can 
lead to increased operating costs and reduced production output.
Water stress/
scarcity
Hazard pattern: 
Chronic 
Production challenges
Water is critical across various stages of cement production, from cooling equipment of rotary kilns, VRMs/
ball mills and compressors, among others. Mill sprays and dust suppression in material handling areas to the 
quenching process in white cement manufacturing. Water scarcity can disrupt these processes, leading to 
reduced efficiency in production output and increased costs.
Increased costs
As freshwater availability becomes increasingly constrained, the cost of sourcing and managing water 
continues to rise. This includes expenses for water tankers, borewell maintenance, treatment infrastructure 
and water recycling systems. This translates into higher operational expenditure, especially during peak 
summer months when municipal or ground supplies are under stress. Furthermore, to address water scarcity 
challenge, additional finances might be required for adopting measures such as water recycling systems, dry 
process kilns and air-based cooling methods.
Heat stress
Hazard pattern: 
Chronic 
Worker safety
Extreme heat presents serious health and safety challenges for workers, particularly in industrial 
environments where tasks are performed near heat-emitting sources like rotatory kiln, clinker cooler unit 
hoods, furnaces. With increased ambient temperature and continuous exposure to heat emitting sources, 
might increase the risk and lead to heat exhaustion, dehydration, heatstroke, etc.
Extreme weather 
events (storms/
strong wind)
Hazard pattern: 
Chronic
Damage to infrastructure
High gusting winds and intense storms result in significant damage to cement plant infrastructure, including 
sheet roofs and windbreaking sheets, among others.
Power outages
Storms and strong winds can cause disruption in transmission systems. This can potentially lead to significant 
power outages and production delays. This is especially likely when power is sourced from common grids, 
unlike captive power plants that offer a more controlled way of power supply.
Health and safety concerns
Extreme weather events pose significant hazards to the safety of employees working in open areas of 
factory premises. Furthermore, extreme weather events carry flying debris which can potentially endanger 
workers and increase chances of bodily injuries, especially for those operating in open yards, quarries or near 
heavy machinery.

At JK Cement, we recognise that a robust risk management architecture is

Risk management
Risk management process
Our risk management is guided by a Board approved 
policy that promotes a proactive approach, integrating 
risk oversight into core processes to safeguard value and 
capture opportunities.
The Board and senior management, supported by 
the Risk Management Committee (RMC), oversee risk 
governance through structured reviews. We follow a dual 
approach:
•	 Bottom up: Functional leaders act as risk owners, 
identifying and managing risks at source.
•	 Top down: RMC and leadership provide strategic 
oversight of macro, regulatory and long term risks, 
ensuring organisational resilience.
The risk framework integrates strategic, operational, 
financial, environmental and compliance aspects to 
support informed decisions and balanced risk taking. 
Internal Audit provides independent assurance on 
controls and risk processes.
Integrated with corporate strategy, our ERM, based on 
the COSO ERM 2004 model and insights from the World 
Economic Forum’s Global Risks Report, covers long term, 
medium term and event driven risks, enabling proactive 
identification and continuous updates to the risk register.
Through systematic risk identification and management, 
we go beyond safeguarding assets to drive performance, 
innovation and resilience. Risks are assessed based on 
likelihood and impact, with periodic capability reviews 
and targeted mitigation. Senior leadership actively 
oversees and reviews the process, ensuring continuous 
improvement.
Integration with strategy 
and business plan
At JK Cement, we embed risk awareness across our 
culture and operations, supported by strong Board 
oversight of economic, ESG and technological shifts.
Risk management is a shared responsibility, strengthened 
through training and a robust bottom‑up process, where 
functional leaders identify and manage risks at source.
Each risk is assessed across financial and non‑financial 
dimensions and embedded into product lifecycles. Using 
a 5×5 matrix, continuous monitoring, climate scenario 
analysis and water‑risk tools, we enhance resilience and 
decision‑making.

This segment is expected to grow by ~7%, primarily driven by 
rising demand from rural housing. Recent GST reforms, lower 
interest rates, and the Government's focus on agricultural 
development through schemes such as the PM Dhan Dhaanya 
Krishi Yojana are expected to enhance liquidity and support 
rural housing growth. Additionally, improved execution under 
the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G) scheme 
is likely to provide further impetus. Urban housing activity is 
expected to remain moderate due to a slowdown in the real 
estate sector, despite lower interest rates and tax rate cuts. 
However, under PMAY-U, growth during FY 2025-26 was 
supported by a higher number of under-construction units 
and project sanctions.

GLOBAL ECONOMY
The global economy is expected to maintain steady growth, 
with global GDP anticipated to expand by 3.3% in 2026 and 
3.2% in 2027. These projections reflect a balance between 
emerging growth drivers and persistent macroeconomic 
challenges. While trade policy uncertainties and geopolitical 
tensions continue to pose risks, these headwinds are 
being partially offset by surging investments in technology, 
especially artificial intelligence (AI), supportive fiscal policies 
and the resilience of the private sector. 
The global outlook remains subject to downside risks. 
Escalating trade disputes, prolonged geopolitical conflicts, 
elevated public debt levels, and larger fiscal deficits could exert 
pressure on long-term interest rates and, in turn, on broader 
financial conditions, thereby adversely affecting financial 
markets, supply chains, and commodity prices. On the 
upside, accelerated AI adoption could translate into strong 
productivity gains, and easing trade tensions could provide 
additional impetus to economic growth. Against this backdrop, 
policymakers remain focused on preserving macroeconomic 
stability, restoring fiscal buffers and advancing structural 
reforms that support sustainable growth.

Advanced economies
Growth in advanced economies is projected at 1.8% in 2026. 
The US economy is expected to grow at a rate of 2.4% in 2026, 
supported by favourable fiscal policies, lower policy rates and a 
gradual moderation in the impact of higher trade barriers.
In the Eurozone, growth forecast is to remain steady at 
1.3% and 1.4% in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Expansion is 
expected to remain subdued due to unresolved structural 
challenges, limited benefits from the recent technology-driven 
investment cycle and the lingering impact of elevated energy 
costs following the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Manufacturing 
activity is also likely to remain under pressure due to currency 
appreciation and competition concerns.
Emerging markets and developing 
economies
Emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) are 
projected to sustain growth of just above 4.0% during 2026 
and 2027, continuing to outpace advanced economies.
China’s economy is expected to grow by 4.5% in 2026, 
supported by fiscal stimulus measures, policy support for 
investment and lending, and relatively lower US effective 
tariff rates on Chinese goods as a result of the year-long trade 
agreement reached in November and stimulus measures that 
are assumed to be implemented over a period of two years. 
In India, GDP growth is projected to be moderate at ~6.6% in 
2027.
Global trade outlook
World trade volume growth is expected to decline from 
4.6% in 2025 to 1.9% in 2026 expected to improve 
marginally to 2.6% in 2027. The slowdown primarily 
reflects adjustments to trade policies, supply chain 
realignments and the normalisation of trade flows 
following periods of front-loaded demand. 
INDIAN ECONOMY 
India remained one of the fastest-growing major economies, 
with GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY 2025-26. However, 
El Niño in the Pacific Ocean is causing significant threat to 
economic activity across India in FY 2026-27. The India 
Meteorological Department (IMD) projected rainfall should 
be lower and restricted to be around 90% of the Long Period 
Average. This translates to a 60% probability of a below-
normal season, raising major concerns for agriculture, 
food inflation, and the broader economy. As a result, GDP is 
projected to moderate to 6.6% as per RBI revised estimate in 
FY 2026-27 amid evolving global economic & warm climate 
conditions, geopolitical uncertainties and external inflationary 
pressures, along with rising crude oil prices over $ 110 per 
barrel much higher than March 26 exit of $ 85 per barrel. 
In February 2026, India and the United States strengthened 
bilateral trade relations through a new trade agreement that 
reduced US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18% with 
immediate effect. This has impacted 55% of India’s $ 87 billion 
exports to the US, excluding priority sectors, such as pharma, 
semiconductor, energy and critical minerals. In exchange, 
India has agreed to move towards zero tariffs and halt Russian 
crude oil purchases. 
Despite these positive developments, the economic outlook 
remains exposed to external risks. Rising geopolitical turmoil 
in West Asia, including the war between the US and Iran, has 
raised concerns over energy security and crude oil price 
volatility. Given India’s substantial dependence on imported 
crude oil, sustained disruptions to global energy supply 
chains could lead to higher input costs, elevated inflation and 
increased pressure. 
In addition, exchange rate volatility and depreciation of the 
Indian rupee could further push up inflation by increasing the 
cost of energy and other essential import items. Nevertheless, 
strong domestic demand, ongoing infrastructure investments, 
policy reforms and a resilient financial system are expected to 
continue supporting India's long-term growth trajectory. 
INDIAN CEMENT INDUSTRY 
Cement demand rebounded in FY 2025-26, with the industry 
expanding by 7-8%. Growth was led by the rural housing, 
industrial and commercial segments, while infrastructure 
activity remained steady. In the upcoming year as well, 
demand is expected to surge by 7-8%, with infrastructure 
activity anticipated to witness a marginal uptick.
The industry added ~65 MnTPA of capacity in FY 2025-26, 
taking the overall installed cement capacity to ~730 MnTPA. 
In FY 2026-27, capacity addition of roughly 75 MnTPA is 
anticipated, driven by favourable demand prospects. However, 
this may moderate following the recent announcements by 
certain industry players to pause expansion plans. The eastern 
region is expected to account for the largest share of capacity 
additions, followed by the northern and western regions. 
The operating rate stood at ~74% in FY 2025-26. Despite 
continued demand growth, the operating rate is likely to 
moderate to around 72% in FY 2026-27 due to significant 
capacity additions. Between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31, the 
industry is anticipated to add nearly 250 MnTPA of capacity, 
with total installed capacity reaching ~975 MnTPA by the end 
of FY 2030-31. Operating rates are projected to average at 
~75% between FY 2025-26 and FY 2030-31, compared with 
~68% over the previous six years.
Most of the planned capacity additions are being undertaken 
by large and mid-sized players with strong financial positions, 
backed by cash surpluses and comfortable gearing levels, 
providing them with the flexibility to raise debt for expansion.

JK CEMENT’S SUSTAINABILITY 
JOURNEY
As part of its commitment to sustainable growth and nation-
building, JK Cement has aligned its growth strategy with global 
sustainability priorities while contributing to India’s transition 
towards a low-carbon economy. Our sustainability framework 
is anchored in four pillars: climate, waste as a resource, 
environment, and people and communities - each of which 
supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. 
Performance of major sustainability KPIs
•	 Green energy mix and thermal substitution: A key 
pillar of JKCL’s decarbonisation approach is its captive 
power infrastructure. As of FY 2025-26, the Company 
is supported by 119.3 MW of Waste Heat Recovery 
Systems (WHRS) capacity and 171.41 MW of renewable 
energy capacity secured through long-term PPAs. 
The Company has set a target of achieving a 75% green 
energy (renewable energy and WHRS) mix compared 
to 19% in the base year FY 2019-20, and a thermal 
substitution rate (TSR) of 35% by FY 2029-30. In FY 2025-
26, the share of green energy reached 51.8%, while TSR 
stood at 11.97%. 
•	 Circular economy: Embracing a robust circular 
economy model, JK Cement is increasing the use of 
industrial by-products, such as fly ash from power plants 
and slag from steel units, in cement manufacturing to 
minimise clinker consumption. The Company is also 
substituting virgin limestone with these materials and 
scaling the use of Alternative Fuels and Raw Materials 
(AFR) within its kilns, preserving critical natural resources 
and diminishing the carbon footprint of its production 
processes.
•	 Water stewardship: Recognising water as a precious 
and finite natural resource, JK Cement is optimising 
its use across operations. Through the adoption of 
water-efficient technologies, including the replacement 
of water-cooled condensers with air-cooled ones at 
its power plants, the Company has improved water 
efficiency across operations. These efforts, coupled with 
water conservation initiatives undertaken both within 
and beyond operational boundaries, have improved the 
Company’s water positivity ratio from 3.2x in the base 
year FY 2019-20 to 4.9x in FY 2025-26, keeping it on 
track to achieve its target of being 5x water positive by 
FY 2029-30. During the year, the Nimbahera Integrated 
Unit has been awarded the ‘Gold Rated’ status under the 
CII Blue Rating System.

In line with the Company's strategic priority to

footprint, FY 2025-26 was a landmark year for capacity 
augmentation. Driven by stringent execution, the 
Company successfully expanded its total Grey Cement 
capacity to 32.26 MnTPA by the close of the financial year.
Building on the successful commissioning of the 
Prayagraj grinding unit in June 2024 and the execution of 
the Mahan Coal Block agreement in May 2024 to secure 
long-term fuel visibility, the Company successfully 
executed the following key projects during the year 
under review:

−The Company successfully commissioned 3.3 
MnTPA Clinker Line-2 at Panna with increase in 
cement grinding capacity by 1 MnTPA each at 
existing locations of Panna, Prayagraj and Hamirpur 
(Total 3 MnTPA) in Q3 and Q4 FY 2025-26.
	
−Further, 3 MnTPA greenfield grinder unit was 
commissioned in Buxar, Bihar during Q4 FY 2025-26 
deepening our presence in Eastern India.

was also commissioned during Q4 FY2025-26.
•	 Ujjain Debottlenecking: Maximising asset utilisation, 
the Company completed a strategic debottlenecking 
initiative at the Ujjain grinding unit, enhancing its 
capacity from 1.5 MnTPA to 2.0 MnTPA in Q1 FY 2025-26.

Future Outlook and Vision 2030
Your Company remains steadfast in its ambition to rank 
among the top-tier cement manufacturers in the country. 
Driven by an aggressive and disciplined capital allocation 
strategy, the Company has set a definitive target to 
reach a total cement production capacity of 50 MnTPA by 
FY 2029-30.
To further solidify market leadership and cater to rising 
infrastructure demand the Company is undertaking 
7 MnTPA Greenfield Expansion through its flagship 
H 4,805 Crore mega-project (comprising 4 MnTPA Clinker 
and 3 MnTPA Cement capacity) at Jaisalmer along with 
two split cement grinding units having a capacity of 
2 MnTPA each at Bikaner and Bhatinda. The project is 
advancing as per schedule, with commissioning targeted 
by H1 FY 2027-28.

portfolio through the new 0.6 MnTPA Nathdwara wall 
putty plant which is progressing well and is scheduled for 
commissioning in Q2 FY 2026-27.
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
The Company remains committed to creating 
sustainable value for the communities in and around its 
areas of operation through focused Corporate Social 
Responsibility (CSR) initiatives in accordance with its 
CSR and Sustainability Policy.
During the year under review, the Company spent H 24.31 
Crores on CSR activities, benefiting over 5.62 lakh 
individuals across rural and underserved communities. 
The Company's interventions were implemented 
across its key thematic areas of Health, Education, 
Environmental Protection and Sustainability, Rural 
Transformation, Livelihood, and Emergency Response 
Services. These initiatives were aligned with relevant 
United Nations SDGs, including Good Health and Well-
being, Quality Education, Gender Equality, Clean Water 
and Sanitation, Climate Action, Economic Growth, and 
Reduced Inequalities.
Education and livelihood continued to be the Company's 
key focus areas. Through its education initiatives, the 
Company supported public schools in and around its 
manufacturing locations to improve access to quality 
education and strengthen learning environments. 
Livelihood interventions focused on enhancing farmers' 
incomes, promoting improved livestock management 
practices, equipping women and youth with market-
relevant skills, and creating sustainable income-
generation opportunities. The Company also contributed 
towards improving rural infrastructure to enhance 
the quality of life in communities and supported both 
preventive and curative healthcare services around its 
manufacturing units.
During the year, the Company implemented several 
impactful initiatives across its areas of operation. 
These included the Adarsh Gram Initiative aimed at 
promoting holistic rural development; support for 
the HOPE School Construction Project to improve 
educational opportunities for first-generation learners; 
the Jeevika Initiative in Buxar, Bihar, focused on skilling 
and livelihood enhancement for women and young girls; 
and the Renal Care Project at Safdarjung Hospital, New 
Delhi, aimed at strengthening access to quality curative 
healthcare. In addition, the Company undertook various 
other programmes aligned with its identified CSR 
thematic areas.
The Company places significant emphasis on measuring 
the effectiveness and outcomes of its CSR interventions. 
Through periodic monitoring, field assessments, 
and impact evaluations, the Company endeavors to 
assess the reach and effectiveness of its initiatives 
and incorporate learnings to enhance their long-term 
sustainability and impact.
