CONVERGING 
PRIORITIES, 
COMMON 
PURPOSE
A sustainability issue is material if 
it significantly impacts society or 
the environment and influences 
a company’s value drivers, 
competitiveness and long-term 
value creation. Material ESG issues 
affect operations, cash flows, 
compliance and capital access, 
while shaping reputation and 
stakeholder relationships, often 
translating external impacts into 
internal financial outcomes.
Materiality assessment
Our approach to materiality
We initiated our first comprehensive materiality 
assessment in FY 2020-21, followed by an impact 
assessment in FY 2024-25, and a double materiality 
assessment in FY 2025-26 to identify financial and 
impact priorities. Inputs from internal and external 
stakeholders were incorporated, with outcomes 
embedded into ERM and approved by top leadership.
Our materiality assessment process
The assessment methodology was designed to comply with 
CSRD standards while integrating JK Cement’s existing

risk 
universe and insights from previous materiality assessments. 
This approach ensured consistency in evaluating financial 
risks and broadened the scope to include a comprehensive 
analysis of sustainability-related impacts and opportunities.
Scope and contextualise
We define our boundaries and operating context 
by reviewing legal and financial structures to 
identify CSRD‑covered entities. We also map our 
value chain to understand stakeholders and our 
operating environment.
Identify ESG topics
We identify a broad set of ESG issues by analysing 
global standards, sector trends and internal 
strategies, supported by peer benchmarking and 
risk databases.
Build the longlist
We consolidate and map issues to ESRS 
sub‑topics, creating a structured longlist. 
We engage stakeholders to assess relevance, 
value chain positioning and potential impacts.
Assess IROs
We identify impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) 
using dual materiality, evaluating environmental/
social outcomes and financial implications, to guide 
action and value creation.
Score and engage
We score each IRO using ESRS criteria and validate 
through stakeholder consultations across five 
groups to ensure balanced perspectives.
Set thresholds
We apply defined thresholds for each stakeholder 
group to finalise material topics, while allowing 
strategic elevation where required five groups to 
ensure balanced perspectives.
Finalise and map
We refine the final list and map it on a materiality 
matrix, showcasing priorities across impact and 
financial dimensions.

social performance.

framework that integrates climate‑related risks and 
opportunities into its core business strategy. Oversight 
rests with our Board of Directors, supported by the CSR

Creating long-term shareholder value
Our approach to shareholder value creation is rooted in disciplined growth, earnings resilience, prudent financial management 
and responsible expansion. During FY 2025-26, we delivered strong volume growth, improved operating scale and resilient 
profitability while continuing to invest in our growth pipeline. Reflecting the strength of our financial performance and confidence 
in future cash flows, the Board recommended a final dividend of I 20 per equity share, up 33.3% over the previous year. 
The successful commissioning of our 6 MnTPA cement capacity expansion, addition of 1.5 MnTPA through debottlenecking 
and another 0.42 MnTPA by acquisition of Saifco Cement (P) Ltd., further strengthens our growth platform and supports long-
term value creation through enhanced scale, market

reach and operating leverage. Going forward, sustained emphasis on cost 
leadership and achieving industry-benchmark EBITDA per tonne is expected to strengthen profitability and drive long-term 
shareholder value.
Responsible tax conduct
We follow a Board-approved tax governance framework 
that guides responsible and transparent tax conduct 
across jurisdictions. Our tax positions are grounded in 
genuine commercial substance, and all related-party 
transactions are conducted on an arm’s length principle.
We do not engage in artificial profit shifting or structures 
lacking economic rationale. Oversight by senior 
management and the Board supports regulatory 
alignment, effective risk management and long-term 
stakeholder confidence.
Deploying capital with discipline
Our capital deployment during FY 2025-26 focused on 
strengthening manufacturing capacity, market access, 
value-added products and long-term competitiveness. 
The expansion programme undertaken during the year 
was completed with approximately 10% savings against 
the planned project cost of I 2,850 Crores, reflecting 
strong project governance and capital efficiency.
Capital expenditure up to 31st March 2026 
comprised I 914 Crores for the greenfield expansion in 
North, whereas I 100 Crores have been spent on the 
6 Lakhs TPA wall putty facility at Nathdwara.
Planned capex of I 3,500-4,000 Crores in FY 2026‑27 
and I 2,000-2,500 Crores in FY 2027-28, including 
sustenance and coal block-related investments, will result 
in additional capacity, coal availability at competitive 
cost and investment in renewable power. This will help in 
increasing earning of the company.
Improving return visibility
Incremental clinker and grinding capacity commissioned 
and under execution enhance operating leverage potential 
as utilisation levels normalise. As several capacities were 
commissioned in the final quarter of FY 2025-26, the full 
benefits of optimal utilisation are expected to be realised 
in the upcomi

ng fiscal year.
As newly commissioned units stabilise, improved fixed-
cost absorption and logistics optimisation are expected 
to strengthen return visibility on deployed capital. The full 
operating detail of these capacity additions is covered in the 
Operational excellence.
Growing through a stronger  
balance sheet
FY 2025-26 further strengthened our financial position, 
supported by enhanced retained earnings and prudent capital 
management. Net worth increased by 15.2% to I 6,961 Crores, 
while book value per share rose by 15.2% to I 901, reflecting 
continued value accretion for shareholders. Despite major 
expansion projects, long-term borrowing increased marginally 
from I 5,103 Crores as on 31st March 2025 to I 5,136 Crores, 
reflecting our ability to generate cash and use of internal 
accruals to fund our capex programmes. 
Strengthening cost resilience
During FY 2025-26, higher production volumes and 
capacity additions led to increased power and fuel, freight 
and forwarding, and employee costs. We mitigated these 
pressures through operational efficiencies, logistics 
optimisation, improved asset utilisation and greater 
manufacturing integration. Investments in waste heat 
recovery, renewable energy and AFR.

supported by safety audits, risk assessments and capability-building programmes. During FY 2025-26, engineering controls, 
automation-led interventions and awareness initiatives across grey cement operations reduced critical risk exposure and 
reinforced safe behaviour.
Governance and management systems
At JK Cement, the health, safety and well-being of our 
people remain a core priority. Our Occupational Health and 
Safety (OHS) Policy, overseen by the Board of Directors, 
applies across all manufacturing operations, grinding 
units and corporate offices, covering 100% of permanent 
employees, contractors and third-party workers under our 
supervision. We comply with applicable national regulations, 
statutory requirements and international standards, including 
ISO 45001:2018.
Our OHS framework promotes active worker participation 
through site-level Safety Committees, safety circles and 
hazard-identification forums. We continuously strengthen 
our systems throug

h benchmarking, structured annual 
safety action plans and risk-based corrective and preventive 
measures. To advance our Zero Harm ambition, we track key 
leading and lagging indicators, including LTIFR, near-miss 
reporting and safety training hours, while maintaining time-
bound improvement targets.

risk elimination and a strong safety culture through risk 
mitigation, continuous inspections and independent validation.

manufacturing operations and limestone mines, with identified

and linked to improvement targets. Emergency preparedness 
is supported through mock drills, response teams and 
regularly updated response manuals, while central and plant-

occupational diseases are subject to a standardised 
investigation process, including root-cause analysis and 
corrective and preventive actions to prevent recurrence.

through OHS criteria embedded in procurement policies and 
vendor agreements. Regular capability-building and safety 
awareness programmes are conducted for employees, 
workers, visitors and logistics partners. To strengthen 
governance, our manufacturing units are independently 
audited and certified to ISO 45001:2018 (occupational health 
and safety standards). As applicable, these systems are also 
integrated with wider ISO-aligned management frameworks 
covering quality, environment and energy management.

Key interventions FY 2025-26
Shopfloor safety measures
During the year, we introduced a range of shopfloor safety 
interventions focused on reducing high-risk exposures, 
enhancing operational controls and improving the safety of 
employees, contractors and visitors.
Reducing electrical hazards
At Aligarh, we introduced remote HT panel switching, face-
recognition access at electrical load centres, insulation coating 
of floors and street poles, and targeted electrical safety 
measures, reducing electrical burn and electrocution risks.
Improving truck unloading
At Hamirpur, boom barrier interlocking with the BRU truck 
tippler system strengthened tippler-area safety by restricting 
access during unloading, reducing manual dependence and 
allowing entry only when safe.
Improving internal traffic
At Aligarh, we introduced hard barricading and vehicle 
diversion measures to improve movement discipline, reduce 
congestion and strengthen operational safety.
Fire and AFR-risk management
During the year, we strengthened fire-risk controls in selected 
AFR-handling areas th

rough integrated detection, monitoring 
and suppression systems designed to improve emergency 
response readiness.
Strengthening odour control and fire safety
We implemented an integrated odour-control and fire-
suppression system with organic enzyme-based spraying, 
reducing odours by ~90%, enabling faster response and 
strengthening workplace safety and the community interface.
Improving fire detection and suppression
We installed an integrated fire detection and suppression 
system across shredder sheds, storage zones, belt conveyors, 
the DG house and process-transfer points, combining UV-IR 
flame detectors, heat detectors, thermal cameras, sprinklers 
and centralised monitoring.
Behaviour-led and participative culture
Safety performance depends not only on engineering 
controls, but also on daily behaviour, ownership and workforce 
participation. During FY 2025-26, we strengthened safety 
culture through dialogue, visible leadership, speak-up systems, 
ownership models and plant-level behavioural interventions. 
We deepened our safety culture through Chai Pe Charcha, 
enabling Visible Felt Leadership (VFL) through dialogue 
between Unit Heads and frontline teams. Storytelling and 
safety narratives linked workplace behaviour with family and 
community well-being, strengthening personal ownership and 
a Safety-First mindset.
At JK White Cement Works, Gotan, we strengthened 
shared safety ownership through the Roko–Toko–Sudhar 
Karo campaign: Roko to stop unsafe acts, Toko to question 
risks and Sudhar Karo to correct them collaboratively. 
This democratised safety, reinforced active intervention and 
reduced at-risk behaviours. At the Nimbahera integrated 
plant, we recognise outstanding contributions to safety by 
selecting a ‘Safety Person of the Month’ from both employee 
and worker categories, honouring their efforts in implementing 
safety initiatives.
Strengthening participative safety
Project YATRA, introduced in July 2025, combines 
capability building,

critical activity identification, SOPs, 
inspections, ten cardinal safety rules, area ownership, 
safety gate meetings, sensitisation and recognition to 
strengthen behavioural safety, workplace ownership 
and compliance discipline.

Key projects and technological interventions
	
	
Carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) 
As part of our steadfast commitment to achieving Net 
Zero by 2070, we have transitioned into a critical phase 
of technological intervention through carbon capture 
and utilisation (CCU). Recognising that process-related 
emissions are the most ‘hard-to-abate’ in cement 
manufacturing, we have spearheaded a flagship 2 TPD 
(tonnes per day) CCU pilot project in collaboration with 
the National Council for Cement and Building Materials 
(NCCBM) and IIT Roorkee. Unlike conventional post-
combustion capture, our innovative approach focuses 
on oxygen-based calcination. 
This process involves utilising oxygen-enriched air in 
the calciner to increase the concentration of CO2 in 
the flue gas. This efficiently isolates the CO2 stream, 
which is then diverted for high-value utilisation rather 
than storage. The captured CO2 is integrated into 
the production of lightweight concrete products and 
olefins, effectively locking the carbon into the built 
environment and creating a circular value chain.
Steel slag reborn 
This initiative tackles the hard-to-abate carbon 
footprints of both steelmaking and cement production 
simultaneously. JK Cement and Tata Steel have 
formed a strategic industrial alliance under the global 
LeadIT initiative to drive circular economy solutions. 
The partnership centers on a high-profile collaborative 
project with Sweden's Cemvis

ion and IIT-ISM Dhanbad 
to commercially process low-grade steel waste, 
specifically Basic Oxygen Furnace (BOF) slag, which 
is traditionally difficult to recycle. By using advanced 
thermal modification, they reclaim valuable residual 
metals for Tata Steel while transforming the remaining 
slag into a highly reactive raw material for JK Cement. 
This cross-industry symbiosis allows JK Cement 
to drastically lower its clinker-to-cement ratio and 
process emissions, while simultaneously shrinking 
Tata Steel's industrial waste footprint.
Air emissions
Air emissions management remains a key focus area within 
our environmental agenda. As a cement manufacturer, our 
operations emit sulphur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx) 
and particulate matter (PM), which are controlled through 
electrostatic precipitators (ESPs), bag houses and bag filters 
installed across our manufacturing facilities. Continuous 
monitoring systems has been installed for real-time monitoring 
of stack emissions and ambient air quality. Various process 
optimisation and technology upgrades also support in 
compliance with the prescribed regulatory standards. 
We comply with conditions stipulated in various regulatory 
permissions, such as Environment Clearance (EC), Consent to 
Establish (CTE), Consent to Operate (CTO), etc, across all our 
sites. During the reporting year, ozone-depleting substance 
(ODS) emissions remained minimal at 0.03 MT of CFC-11 
equivalent. Further, we have third-party monitoring through 
NABL-accredited labs.

BIODIVERSITY
Biodiversity conservation is integral to our approach to responsible growth and environmental stewardship. Guided by our 
Biodiversity Policy, we implement site-specific action plans developed in collaboration with local stakeholders and expert teams. 
Our approach aligns with the CII-India Business & Biodiversity Initiative (IBBI) and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity 
Framework. We assess projects using the mitigation hierarchy of avoid, minimise, restore and offset to manage biodiversity 
impacts effectively. We maintain a strict prohibition on involvement in the trade of CITES-listed species and work to prevent 
adverse impacts on threatened flora and fauna. Ecosystem restoration, native species plantation and the development of 
self-sustaining green corridors remain key focus areas.
Operational footprint and site sensitivity
We m

anage a significant land area ~8,400 hectares across 
13 operational sites, including manufacturing cement plants, 
grinding units and mines. We recognise that our presence 
in these landscapes carries a responsibility to monitor 
and mitigate our ‘inside-out’ impacts. While none of our 
mentioned operations are located within notified protected 
areas or high-biodiversity value zones, we maintain a policy 
of heightened vigilance for sites near sensitive ecosystems. 
Biodiversity risk assessment
Before any project expansion or initiation, we conduct 
comprehensive environmental impact assessments (EIAs) 
that analyse biodiversity within a 10-kilometre radius of 
project boundaries. These studies result in preparation 
of site-specific wildlife management plans (WMPs) in 
consultation with local authorities with clear, time-bound 
conservation targets.
Our Panna integrated plant is located ~13 km from the 
Panna Tiger Reserve, this site is a priority location for 
our management teams, from biodiversity conservation 
perspective. In addition to implementation of site-specific 
wildlife conservation plan, we have also initiated biodiversity 
risk assessment at this location in line with TNFD LEAP 
Approach. The results of this study indicate no negative 
impact of our operations on the ecosystem.
Biodiversity assessment: The LEAP 
approach
During FY 2025-26, we initiated assessing the dependency- 
and impact- related biodiversity risk covering our own 
operations and adjacent areas covering an aerial radius 
of 10 km. We have initiated a location-specific approach 
in Nimbahera, Mangrol and Panna. This methodology is 
aligned with TNFD’s LEAP approach. The methodology 
allows us to systematically analyse its dependencies and 
impacts on natural resources, evaluate potential risks and 
identify opportunities for positive contributions. By applying 
the LEAP approach, the units integrate nature-related 
considerations into operational and strategic planning, 
ensuring

that sustainability and ecological resilience remain 
central to decision-making. To manage our environmental 
dependencies, we have adopted the TNFD-aligned LEAP 
methodology, integrating nature-related risks directly into 
our corporate strategy.
Locate (geographic interface)
We map our operational footprint against local 
ecosystems to establish detailed biodiversity 
baselines. This stage identifies proximity to 
protected areas (PAs), key biodiversity areas (KBAs) 
and other sites of high conservation importance to 
ensure geographic sensitivity.
2
Evaluate (dependencies and Impacts)
We apply a dual ‘inside-out’ and ‘outside-in’ 
assessment. We evaluate how much our operations 
depend on ecosystem services (e.g. water and 
climate regulation) and the corresponding impact 
our activities have on natural capital. This materiality 
matrix prioritises the most critical ecosystem 
services for sustainable management.
3
Assess (risks and opportunities) 
Using a dependency-impact matrix, we classify 
nature-related risks from very high to low. This 
identifies physical, regulatory and reputational 
threats while uncovering opportunities in 
biodiversity stewardship and nature-positive 
practices. These findings are integrated into 
our multi-disciplinary, organisation-wide risk 
management processes.
4
Prepare (response and integration) 
We develop site-specific biodiversity management 
plans (BMP). Mitigation follows a strict hierarchy: 
avoid, minimise, restore and offset for any residual 
impacts. This ensures that nature-positive 
outcomes are embedded in our long-term financial 
and operational planning.
To systematically identify and manage nature-related 
dependencies, impacts, risks, and opportunities (DIRO), 
we utilise the TNFD's LEAP framework alongside global 
tools like the WRI Ecosystem Services Review and the WWF 
Biodiversity Risk Filter.

E tool, we identified that our manufacturing

Opportunities
We strategically transform environmental challenges into 
business opportunities to build long-term resilience:
Resource efficiency and circular economy
By reducing our reliance on virgin natural resources (like

Access to new markets

positioning ourselves to benefit from emerging green credits 
markets which could provide additional revenue streams.
Ecosystem restoration and net gain
Investing in nature-based solutions, such as converting 
exhausted mine pits into vital water reservoirs for migratory 
birds and developing the 50-hectare Biodiversity Park in

community goodwill.

Methodology
We conducted Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) studies across 
our major operational boundaries, including Nimbahera, 
Mangrol and Muddapur plants, covering multiple cement 
variants. Using a cradle-to-gate approach, the assessment 
evaluated environmental impacts from raw material extraction 
and transportation through manufacturing and emissions, up 
to the factory gate, with one tonne of cement as the functional 
unit. Based on the ReCiPe LCIA methodology, the study 
assessed impacts across categories including GHG emissions, 
ozone depletion, particulate matter formation, acidification, 
eutrophication, land use and human health. The assessment 
confirmed that blended cements such as PPC, PSC and 
composite cement have significantly lower environmental 
impacts than OPC, supporting our low-carbon product 
strategy and decarbonisation roadmap while strengthening 
data-driven environmental decision-making.

Climate risk assessment 
To have a strategic response to mitigate the impact of climate 
change induced risks, we have undertaken a comprehensive 
climate risk assessment for our operations across India. 
Based on the outcome of the assessments, risk mitigation 
recommendations and measures were designed and 
inculcated in our ov

erall business strategy to minimise the

In this context, Climate Change Risk assessment (CCRA) 
serves as a foundational step for the company, not only 
towards identification and mitigation of climate-related 
risks but also to seize emerging opportunities. It involves 
a systematic evaluation of both climate change induced, 
physical and transition risks linked to climate change, enabling 
organisations to build long-term resilience and align with global 
disclosure frameworks such as the Task Force on Climate-
related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations and 
IFRS S2 Standard.
Relevance to our business
As the effects of climate change become more evident, 
we face increasing risks such as revenue losses from supply 
chain disruptions and decreased productivity, infrastructural 
damage from extreme weather events, and higher operational 
costs due to stricter environmental regulations. Additionally, 
shifts in market dynamics can impact raw material availability 
and consumer preferences, while reputational risks arise if we 
are perceived as environmentally irresponsible. Implementing 
proactive climate strategies is crucial for JK Cement to 
mitigate these impacts and ensure sustainable growth. 
Conducting a CCRA allows us to proactively manage the 
identified potential risks, along with opportunities and build 
climate resilience across our operations and value chain.

Physical risk
We, at JK Cement, have conducted a comprehensive analysis of climate change that induced hazards for the selected sites/
operations (within the risk assessment boundary) under two selected SSP scenarios as highlighted above. The table below 
highlights key potential climate change induced hazards identified for our operations across India and their potential business

Flood/extreme 
rainfall
Hazard pattern: 
Acute 
Disruption in supply chain
Acute flooding can significantly disrupt the surface transportation of raw materials used in cement 
manufacturing such as limestone, gypsum and coal, leading to potential production delays. Additionally, 
it might further impact on the distribution of the finished product, due to disrupted access to transportation 
and further increased logistics cost.
Operational disruptions
Cement manufacturing plants in flood-prone areas are highly susceptible to significant physical damage from 
waterlogging, which can impact functioning of machinery like crushers, stackers and reclaimers, segregation 
machinery used in raw material handling, among others. Flooding/extreme rainfall can also lead to significant 
water infiltration in industrial facilities, resulting in operational delays, ground-level equipment damage, 
material damage and damage to electrical rooms. Additionally, flooding/extreme rainfall can cause regional 
power outages, resulting in production delays/disruptions.
Economic impact
The cu

mulative effects of these disruptions, supply chain interruptions, facility damage, operational halts can 
lead to increased operating costs and reduced production output.
Water stress/
scarcity
Hazard pattern: 
Chronic 
Production challenges
Water is critical across various stages of cement production, from cooling equipment of rotary kilns, VRMs/
ball mills and compressors, among others. Mill sprays and dust suppression in material handling areas to the 
quenching process in white cement manufacturing. Water scarcity can disrupt these processes, leading to 
reduced efficiency in production output and increased costs.
Increased costs
As freshwater availability becomes increasingly constrained, the cost of sourcing and managing water 
continues to rise. This includes expenses for water tankers, borewell maintenance, treatment infrastructure 
and water recycling systems. This translates into higher operational expenditure, especially during peak 
summer months when municipal or ground supplies are under stress. Furthermore, to address water scarcity 
challenge, additional finances might be required for adopting measures such as water recycling systems, dry 
process kilns and air-based cooling methods.
Heat stress
Hazard pattern: 
Chronic 
Worker safety
Extreme heat presents serious health and safety challenges for workers, particularly in industrial 
environments where tasks are performed near heat-emitting sources like rotatory kiln, clinker cooler unit 
hoods, furnaces. With increased ambient temperature and continuous exposure to heat emitting sources, 
might increase the risk and lead to heat exhaustion, dehydration, heatstroke, etc.
Extreme weather 
events (storms/
strong wind)
Hazard pattern: 
Chronic
Damage to infrastructure
High gusting winds and intense storms result in significant damage to cement plant infrastructure, including 
sheet roofs and windbreaking sheets, among others.
Power outages
Storms and strong winds can cause disruption in transmission sys

tems. This can potentially lead to significant 
power outages and production delays. This is especially likely when power is sourced from common grids, 
unlike captive power plants that offer a more controlled way of power supply.
Health and safety concerns
Extreme weather events pose significant hazards to the safety of employees working in open areas of 
factory premises. Furthermore, extreme weather events carry flying debris which can potentially endanger 
workers and increase chances of bodily injuries, especially for those operating in open yards, quarries or near 
heavy machinery.

AND PROTECTING VALUE
At JK Cement, we recognise that a robust risk management architecture is 
fundamental to maintaining operational excellence and delivering long-term 
shareholder value.
Risk management
Risk management process
Our risk management is guided by a Board approved 
policy that promotes a proactive approach, integrating 
risk oversight into core processes to safeguard value and 
capture opportunities.
The Board and senior management, supported by 
the Risk Management Committee (RMC), oversee risk 
governance through structured reviews. We follow a dual 
approach:
•	 Bottom up: Functional leaders act as risk owners, 
identifying and managing risks at source.
•	 Top down: RMC and leadership provide strategic 
oversight of macro, regulatory and long term risks, 
ensuring organisational resilience.
The risk framework integrates strategic, operational, 
financial, environmental and compliance aspects to 
support informed decisions and balanced risk taking. 
Internal Audit provides independent assurance on 
controls and risk processes.
Integrated with corporate strategy, our ERM, based on 
the COSO ERM 2004 model and insights from th

e World 
Economic Forum’s Global Risks Report, covers long term, 
medium term and event driven risks, enabling proactive 
identification and continuous updates to the risk register.
Through systematic risk identification and management, 
we go beyond safeguarding assets to drive performance, 
innovation and resilience. Risks are assessed based on 
likelihood and impact, with periodic capability reviews 
and targeted mitigation. Senior leadership actively 
oversees and reviews the process, ensuring continuous 
improvement.
Integration with strategy 
and business plan
At JK Cement, we embed risk awareness across our 
culture and operations, supported by strong Board 
oversight of economic, ESG and technological shifts.
Risk management is a shared responsibility, strengthened 
through training and a robust bottom‑up process, where 
functional leaders identify and manage risks at source.
Each risk is assessed across financial and non‑financial 
dimensions and embedded into product lifecycles. Using 
a 5×5 matrix, continuous monitoring, climate scenario 
analysis and water‑risk tools, we enhance resilience and 
decision‑making.

•	 Expanding capacity though greenfield and brownfield project 
across the geographies in high demand regions to mitigate 
the risks associated with regional demand-supply imbalances 
and maintain our growth trajectory
•	 The competition is being tracked and required actions are

is in place to counter the pricing strategies
•	 Periodic review of product wise pricing and schemes run

suppliers under long‑term contracts, enabling economies of

•	 Major raw materials are being procured from the nearest

•	 Orders are placed well in advance after source validation

our dependency on conventional fuels

change risk assessment study to understand the associated 
risks and their potential impacts on our operations across 
different timeframes (short-, medium-, and long-term)

Purchased goods and

183340 Category 1 emissions have been calculated using the spend-bas

37753 Category 2 emissions have been calculated using the spend-based approach.

base year of the US EEIO emission factors.
Fuel-and-energy-
related-activities  
(not included in  
Scope 1 or 2)
1235513 Category 3 emissions have been calculated in accordance with the GHG Protocol 
Technical Guidance using the Average Data method.
The T&D loss percentage for India (~17–19%) is sourced from MoSPI Energy 
Statistics 2025. This is combined with the IEA grid-WTT upstream factor to 
calculate emissions from electricity lost during transmission and distribution.

transportation and 
distribution
648197 Category 4 emissions were calculated using the distance method and spend-
based method as per GHG Protocol Technical Guidance, using DEFRA 2025 and 
India GHG Program mode-specific emission factors.

operations

Protocol Technical Guidance, using DEFRA 2025 Emission Factors
Business travel
837 Emissions are calculated by multiplying the total distance travelled by employees 
(in km) for each travel mode (air, rail, road) with the corresponding mode-specific 
emission factors (kgCO₂e/km) sourced from DEFRA 2025/India GHG Program.
Employee commuting
796 Category 7 emissions were calculated using the distance-based method.
Travel activity data (passenger-km) by mode (air, rail, road) was multiplied with India 
GHG Program mode-specific emission factors, covering both direct and indirect 
emissions.

Management share ownership

IT security and cybersecurity
Board level governance
Our Risk Committee headed by Mr. Paul Heinz Hugentobler is charged with oversight 
and review of risk management and identification of emerging risks. These risks 
include cybersecurity and IT risks as well as periodic risk assessments in these 
aspects.
Executive Management 
Responsibility
Our Chief Digital Officer, who is a part of our Executive Management Team is in charge 
of execution of IT security and cybersecurity across our plants and offices. We are 
ISO 27001 certified organisation. We also implemented VAPT (Vulnerability and 
Penetration Testing) for each and every deployment at JKCL Software through an 
external agency. We also engaged third party agency for Half Yearly Audit of our IT 
security systems.
Supply chain performance
ESG screening
We sign contracts with our vendors and drivers to ensure that ESG aspects like child 
labour, forced labour, hazardous waste spills and biodiversity damage are prevented. 
We also conduct frequent audits of our suppliers to ensure all suppliers are covered 
in a span of three years. While we source most primary raw materials from our leased 
mines, the dependence on suppliers for critical raw material is low.
All our vendors are expected to comply with our ESG Policy and Supplier code of 
conduct to ensure there is no adverse impact due to business operations.

Management Discussion and Analysis
GLOBAL ECONOMY
The global economy is expected to maintain steady growth, 
with global GDP anticipated to expand by 3.3% in 2026 and 
3.2% in 2027. These projections reflect a balance between 
emerging growth drivers and persistent macroeconomic 
challenges. While trade policy uncertainties and geopolitical 
tensions continue to pose risks, these headwinds are 
being partially offset by surging investments in technology, 
especially artificial intelligence (AI), supportive fiscal policies 
and the resilience of the private sector. 
The global outlook remains subject to downside risks. 
Escalating trade disputes, prolonged geopolitical conflicts, 
elevated public debt levels, and larger fiscal deficits could exert 
pressure on long-term interest rates and, in turn, on broader 
financial conditions, thereby adversely affecting financial 
markets, supply chains, and commodity prices. On the 
upside, accelerated AI adoption could translate into strong 
productivity gains, and easing trade tensions could provide 
additional impetus to economic growth. Against this backdrop, 
policymakers remain

focused on preserving macroeconomic 
stability, restoring fiscal buffers and advancing structural 
reforms that support sustainable growth.

Advanced economies
Growth in advanced economies is projected at 1.8% in 2026. 
The US economy is expected to grow at a rate of 2.4% in 2026, 
supported by favourable fiscal policies, lower policy rates and a 
gradual moderation in the impact of higher trade barriers.
In the Eurozone, growth forecast is to remain steady at 
1.3% and 1.4% in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Expansion is 
expected to remain subdued due to unresolved structural 
challenges, limited benefits from the recent technology-driven 
investment cycle and the lingering impact of elevated energy 
costs following the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Manufacturing 
activity is also likely to remain under pressure due to currency 
appreciation and competition concerns.
Emerging markets and developing 
economies
Emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) are 
projected to sustain growth of just above 4.0% during 2026 
and 2027, continuing to outpace advanced economies.
China’s economy is expected to grow by 4.5% in 2026, 
supported by fiscal stimulus measures, policy support for 
investment and lending, and relatively lower US effective 
tariff rates on Chinese goods as a result of the year-long trade 
agreement reached in November and stimulus measures that 
are assumed to be implemented over a period of two years. 
In India, GDP growth is projected to be moderate at ~6.6% in 
2027.
Global trade outlook
World trade volume growth is expected to decline from 
4.6% in 2025 to 1.9% in 2026 expected to improve 
marginally to 2.6% in 2027. The slowdown primarily 
reflects adjustments to trade policies, supply chain 
realignments and the normalisation of trade flows 
following

periods of front-loaded demand. 
INDIAN ECONOMY 
India remained one of the fastest-growing major economies, 
with GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY 2025-26. However, 
El Niño in the Pacific Ocean is causing significant threat to 
economic activity across India in FY 2026-27. The India 
Meteorological Department (IMD) projected rainfall should 
be lower and restricted to be around 90% of the Long Period 
Average. This translates to a 60% probability of a below-
normal season, raising major concerns for agriculture, 
food inflation, and the broader economy. As a result, GDP is 
projected to moderate to 6.6% as per RBI revised estimate in 
FY 2026-27 amid evolving global economic & warm climate 
conditions, geopolitical uncertainties and external inflationary 
pressures, along with rising crude oil prices over $ 110 per 
barrel much higher than March 26 exit of $ 85 per barrel. 
In February 2026, India and the United States strengthened 
bilateral trade relations through a new trade agreement that 
reduced US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18% with 
immediate effect. This has impacted 55% of India’s $ 87 billion 
exports to the US, excluding priority sectors, such as pharma, 
semiconductor, energy and critical minerals. In exchange, 
India has agreed to move towards zero tariffs and halt Russian 
crude oil purchases. 
Despite these positive developments, the economic outlook 
remains exposed to external risks. Rising geopolitical turmoil 
in West Asia, including the war between the US and Iran, has 
raised concerns over energy security and crude oil price 
volatility. Given India’s substantial dependence on imported 
crude oil, sustained disruptions to global energy supply 
chains could lead to higher input costs, elevated inflation and 
increased pressure. 
In addition, exchange rate volatility and depreciation of the 
Indian rupee could further push up inflation by increasing the 
cost of energy and other essential import items. Nevertheless, 
strong domestic

demand, ongoing infrastructure investments, 
policy reforms and a resilient financial system are expected to 
continue supporting India's long-term growth trajectory. 
INDIAN CEMENT INDUSTRY 
Cement demand rebounded in FY 2025-26, with the industry 
expanding by 7-8%. Growth was led by the rural housing, 
industrial and commercial segments, while infrastructure 
activity remained steady. In the upcoming year as well, 
demand is expected to surge by 7-8%, with infrastructure 
activity anticipated to witness a marginal uptick.
The industry added ~65 MnTPA of capacity in FY 2025-26, 
taking the overall installed cement capacity to ~730 MnTPA. 
In FY 2026-27, capacity addition of roughly 75 MnTPA is 
anticipated, driven by favourable demand prospects. However, 
this may moderate following the recent announcements by 
certain industry players to pause expansion plans. The eastern 
region is expected to account for the largest share of capacity 
additions, followed by the northern and western regions. 
The operating rate stood at ~74% in FY 2025-26. Despite 
continued demand growth, the operating rate is likely to 
moderate to around 72% in FY 2026-27 due to significant 
capacity additions. Between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31, the 
industry is anticipated to add nearly 250 MnTPA of capacity, 
with total installed capacity reaching ~975 MnTPA by the end 
of FY 2030-31. Operating rates are projected to average at 
~75% between FY 2025-26 and FY 2030-31, compared with 
~68% over the previous six years.
Most of the planned capacity additions are being undertaken 
by large and mid-sized players with strong financial positions, 
backed by cash surpluses and comfortable gearing levels, 
providing them with the flexibility to raise debt for expansion.

JK CEMENT’S SUSTAINABILITY 
JOURNEY
As part of its commitment to sustainable growth and nation-
building, JK Cement has aligned its growth strategy with global 
sustainability priorities while contributing to India’s transition 
towards a low-carbon economy. Our sustainability framework 
is anchored in four pillars: climate, waste as a resource, 
environment, and people and communities - each of which 
supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. 
Performance of major sustainability KPIs
•	 Green energy mix and thermal substitution: A key 
pillar of JKCL’s decarbonisation approach is its captive 
power infrastructure. As of FY 2025-26, the Company 
is supported by 119.3 MW of Waste Heat Recovery 
Systems (WHRS) capacity and 171.41 MW of renewable 
energy capacity secured through long-term PPAs. 
The Company has set a target of achieving a 75% green 
energy (renewable energy and WHRS) mix compared 
to 19% in the base year FY 2019-20, and a thermal 
substitution rate (TSR) of 35% by FY 2029-30. In FY 2025-
26, the share of green energy reached 51.8%, while TSR 
stood at 11.97%. 
•	 Circular economy: Embracing a robust circular 
economy model, JK Cement is increasing the use of 
industrial by-products, such as fly ash from power plants 
and slag from steel units, in cement manufacturing to 
minimise clinker consumption. The Company is also 
substituting virgin limestone with these materials and 
scaling the use of Alternative Fuels and Raw Materials 
(AFR) within its kilns, preserving critical natural resources 
and diminishing the carbon footprint of its production 
processes.
•	 Water stewardship: Recognising water as a precious 
and finite natural resource, JK Cement is optimising 
its use across operations. Through the adoption of 
water-efficient technologies, including the replac

ement 
of water-cooled condensers with air-cooled ones at 
its power plants, the Company has improved water 
efficiency across operations. These efforts, coupled with 
water conservation initiatives undertaken both within 
and beyond operational boundaries, have improved the 
Company’s water positivity ratio from 3.2x in the base 
year FY 2019-20 to 4.9x in FY 2025-26, keeping it on 
track to achieve its target of being 5x water positive by 
FY 2029-30. During the year, the Nimbahera Integrated 
Unit has been awarded the ‘Gold Rated’ status under the 
CII Blue Rating System.

impact operating margins. The Company mitigates this 
risk through a comprehensive procurement planning that 
encompasses active global sourcing, long-term supply 
agreements, vendor base diversification, and inventory 
optimization. Further, the Company continuously 
monitors commodity prices and rigorously evaluates 
mitigation strategies during monthly management 
review meetings.

A)	 Conservation of Energy
	
Energy efficiency remains a structural lever for J. K. 
Cement Ltd. in strengthening competitiveness and 
advancing our decarbonisation pathway. We focus 
on operational excellence and adopt high-impact, 
low-investment solutions to make measurable 
progress in reducing our environmental footprint.
	
During FY 2025-26, we implemented a series of 
targeted initiatives across our manufacturing units 
to optimize electrical and thermal energy use. 
With a strategic investment of H 65 Crores, these 
projects resulted in a total saving of 1,384 Lakh 
kWh of electricity, equivalent to 11,886 tonnes of oil 
equivalent (TOE) and approximately 70,981 Tonnes 
of CO2. These energy efficiency initiatives have also 
led to substantial cost savings of around H 48 Cr in 
the FY 26 itself and a meaningful reduction in our 
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

These savings 
and reduction in the GHG emissions are recurring in 
nature and will provide the said benefits each year.
	
Our progress in energy management directly 
supports our role as a future-ready organization. 
These initiatives align with the United Nations 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specifically 
supporting Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 
7), Industry and Innovation (SDG 9), Responsible 
Production (SDG 12), and Climate Action (SDG 13). 
By integrating these goals into our daily operations, 
we ensure that our growth remains responsible 
and resilient.
	
Our energy conservation initiatives during the year 
were structured across the following categories:
1.	
Process Optimisation
	
We fine-tune our existing systems, optimize 
process parameters, interlocks, and control logic. 
These improvements were driven by rigorous data 
monitoring and a focus on operational discipline. 
By refining how our plants run on a minute-to-
minute basis, we have enhanced both the reliability 
of our systems and our overall manufacturing 
performance. We have secured significant 
energy reductions without the need for major 
capital investment.
	
The impact of these low-cost, high-return initiatives 
has been substantial. With a modest expenditure 
of H 6 Crores, our process optimization efforts 
delivered around H 17 Crores in savings. This was 
achieved through a reduction of 384 Lakh kWh of 
electricity and a significant decrease in thermal 
energy consumption, totalling 3,298 tonnes of oil 
equivalent (TOE) and approximately 27,234 Tonnes 
of CO2. These results underscore our commitment 
to resource efficiency as a driver of cost leadership.
2.	 Installing of Energy-efficiency Equipment
	
Upgradation of compressors, motors, fans and 
pumps to high-efficiency models lowered auxiliary 
consumption and enhanced electrical system 
performance. These targeted investments delivered 
measurable reduction in unit energy consumption. 
These initiatives collectivel

y delivered an impressive 
overall yearly saving of H 5 Crores achieved with 
reduction of 66 Lakh kWh of electricity equivalent 
to 564 TOE and approximately 4,506 Tonnes of CO2 
with one time expenditure of around H 6 Crores.
3.	
In-house Small Modifications
	
Employee-led continuous improvement initiatives 
focused on compressed air systems, material 
handling circuits and idle-load management also led 
energy savings. The incremental efficiency gains 
collectively delivered substantial energy savings 
without significant capital outlay. As a direct result, 
we have achieved saving of around H 2 Crores with 
reduction of 15 Lakh kWh of electricity equivalent 
to 127 TOE and approximately 1,045 Tonnes of CO2 
with an expenditure of H 0.50 Cr only.
4.	
Downsizing the Existing Equipment
	
To maximize operational efficiency, we conducted 
a thorough review of our motor loading across 
various units. We identified equipment operating 
significantly below their designed capacity and 
replaced them with right-sized, lower-kilowatt 
(kW) alternatives.
	
This optimization ensures that our motors operate 
at their peak efficiency levels, minimizing energy 
wastage and reducing unnecessary power 
consumption. While these modifications required 
negligible investment, they represent our meticulous 
approach to resource management. Collectively, 
these steps resulted in a reduction of 0.36 Lakh kWh 
in electricity consumption equivalent to 3 TOE and 
approximately 26 Tonnes of CO2, contributing to a 
total recurring saving of H 0.02 crore.
5.	
Improving Production and Operational 
Efficiency
	
Optimisation of kiln heat balance, clinker cooler 
performance and reduction in idle running 
hours improved specific heat rate and stabilised 
production efficiency. It includes one time

Has the entity implemented a mechanism for Zero Liquid Discharge? If yes, provide details of its coverage 
and implementation.
	
JK Cement has successfully implemented a robust mechanism for Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) across its 
manufacturing facilities, ensuring that no untreated wastewater is released into the environment. The scope 
covers 100% of the wastewater generated within our plant premises and residential colony. Our implementation 
strategy centres on the operation of advanced Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) and Effluent Treatment Plants 
(ETPs), where wastewater undergoes rigorous multi-stage processing to meet stringent quality standards.
	
The treated water is then systematically integrated back into our industrial cycle, creating a closed-loop system. 
Specifically, the recycled water is repurposed for critical non-potable applications, including industrial cooling 
processes, dust suppression systems, and the maintenance of extensive greenbelt. By prioritizing the recycling 
and reuse of every drop of treated effluent, JK Cement not only ensures ZLD compliance but also significantly 
reduces its fresh water requirements, reinforcing our commitment to sustainable water stewardship.

Lowering the proportion of clinker in cement by producing more blended cement.
	
JK Cement is a core member of LeadIT, a global group launched by the governments of Sweden and India at 
the UN Climate Action Summit. In December 2025, under the LeadIT umbrella, JK Cement was named as a key 
partner in cross-border innovation projects funded by the Swedish Energy Agency and India’s Department of 
Science and Technology.
	
A defining example of circular economy innovation is the collaboration between JK Cement and Tata Steel, 
formally launched in FY 2025-26. Titled “Steel Slag Reborn,” this partnership involves JK Cement, Tata Steel, IIT 
ISM Dhanbad, and Swedish partner Cemvision. The project focuses on recovering high-value metallics from steel 
slag and converting the remaining mineral residue into sustainable supplementary cementitious materials (SCM). 
By using steel slag as a raw material for cement, the partnership addresses two industrial challenges: it reduces 
waste for the steel industry and lowers the clinker requirement (and carbon footprint) for the cement industry.
	
In June 2025, JK Cement made history by becoming the first cement company in India to commence full-

scale commercial production of LC3 (formally known as Portland Limestone Calcined Clay Cement under IS 
18189:2023). This was achieved at Mangrol facility in Rajasthan, moving beyond pilot-scale trials to a mainstream 
industrial product branded as JK Super LC3. By replacing over 50% of carbon-intensive clinker with a blend of 
calcined clay and crushed limestone, JK Cement’s LC3 reduces CO2 emissions by up to 40% as compared to 
traditional OPC product.

JK Cement adopts a circular economy approach to waste management, focusing on the principle of “Waste 
to Wealth.” Across its establishments, the company utilizes a sophisticated Co-processing mechanism where 
hazardous and non-hazardous industrial, agricultural, and municipal wastes are repurposed as Alternative Fuels 
and Raw Materials (AFR). For internal waste, the entity operates on-site Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) and 
Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs) to achieve Zero Effluent Discharge, recycling treated water for industrial cooling 
and greenbelt maintenance.
	
To manage any residual hazardous waste, such as used oil or chemical containers, the entity follows a strict 
protocol of segregation, secure storage, and disposal through Authorized Recyclers approved by the State 
Pollution Control Boards. These practices are governed by a robust Environmental Management System (ISO 
14001), ensuring that toxic footprints are minimized throughout the product lifecycle.

Assurance Methodology 
During the assurance engagement, TUVI adopted a risk-based approach, focusing verification efforts on disclosures and issues of high 
material relevance to JKCL and its stakeholders. The objective was to assess the reliability and accuracy of the non-financial information 
dis

closed, with emphasis on the robustness of data management systems, internal controls, and information flows. In summary, 
evidence was gathered on a risk-based sampling basis: sites, KPIs, and disclosures were selected by reference to materiality, inherent 
risk of misstatement, estimation uncertainty, data complexity, and the relative contribution of each site to the total ESG footprint, 
with locations and indicators of higher inherent risk receiving more extensive testing (the detailed sampling methodology is set out in 
Section 5 below). As part of this approach, TUVI also performed validation of the relevant IT general controls (ITGCs) and ESG 
application controls over the systems used to capture, aggregate, and report the disclosures, including access controls, change

Board Functioning and Procedures
The Board of Directors is committed to ensuring good 
governance through a highly structured and self-governing 
style of functioning. Meetings are conducted in accordance 
with a well-designed agenda, formulated in compliance with 
the Act, and the Secretarial Standards (SS-1) prescribed 
by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI). To 
leverage technology, reduce paper consumption, and 
ensure secure communication, the Company has adopted 
the Dess Digital Meetings Software. Agenda papers, 
comprising comprehensive notes and management 
reports, are circulated digitally at least seven days prior to 
the meeting to facilitate informed decision-making.
Board meetings are attended by all Directors, Company 
Secretary, Business Heads, and Group Financial Controller. 
Depending on business needs, senior executives are invited 
to make presentations on financial performance, strategic 
initiatives etc.
Flow of Information and Post-Meeting Follow-up
The Board is provided with unrestricted access to all 
requisite information to enable effective oversight. The 
Management systematically shares updates on annual 
operating plans, capital budgets, quarterly financial results, 
risk mit

igation strategies, and material regulatory or legal 
developments. Critical and price-sensitive information 
is shared with due confidentiality. Further, the Company 
maintains a robust post-meeting follow-up mechanism. 
Important decisions from the Board and Committee 
meetings are promptly communicated to the respective 
functional departments, and an Action Taken Report 
is placed at subsequent meetings to ensure seamless 
execution and accountability.
Board Support: Role of the Company Secretary
The Company Secretary plays a critical role in facilitating 
the smooth functioning of the Board and its Committees. 
The Company Secretary is responsible for convening 
meetings, distributing the agenda, and recording the 
minutes. Acting as a formalised interface between the 
Board and the Management, the Company Secretary 
provides guidance to the Directors on their legal and 
regulatory responsibilities and ensures the Company's 
compliance with applicable laws including corporate laws, 
securities laws and corporate governance standards.
Separate Meeting of Independent Directors
In compliance with Schedule IV of the Act and Regulation 
25(3) of the Listing Regulations, a separate meeting of the 
Independent Directors was convened on January 16, 2026.
The meeting was held without the presence of Non-
Independent Directors and members of the Management. 
During the meeting, the Independent Directors reviewed 
the performance of the Non-Independent Directors, the 
Board as a whole and the Chairperson of the Company. 
They also assessed the quality, quantity and timeliness 
of the flow of information between the Management and 
the Board and expressed satisfaction that the information 
provided was adequate to enable effective discharge of 
their responsibilities.
The Independent Directors also reviewed the effectiveness 
of the Company’s governance framework, functioning 
of the Board Committees, quality of financial reporting 
and internal control environment, and co

nfirmed that 
they were able to exercise their duties with objective 
and independent judgement. The Independent Directors 
expressed satisfaction with the Company’s governance 
standards, operational execution capabilities and project 
management framework.
Familiarisation and Induction Programme
The Company believes that a well-informed Board is critical 
for robust corporate governance. Upon appointment, 
new Directors undergo induction process covering 
the Company’s history, values, corporate governance 
framework, and business model. Throughout the year, 
the Board is continuously engaged through immersion 
sessions, strategy presentations, and plant visits.
These ongoing programmes familiarise Directors with 
the Company’s manufacturing facets, market presence, 
ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) targets, and 
competitive landscape. The detailed framework of the 
Familiarisation Programme is hosted on the Company’s 
website and can be accessed at: https://www.jkcement.com/.

ensuring the timely receipt of statutory communications 
by shareholders.

ined pending for more

Commodity Price Risk: As a manufacturing entity, 
the Company is exposed to the price volatility of key 
commodities, most notably imported petcoke, coal, and 
putty chemicals. Because fuel is a primary cost driver, any 
adverse fluctuation in its price can significantly impact 
operating margins. The Company mitigates this risk through 
a comprehensive procurement planning that encompasses 
active global sourcing, long-term supply agreements, 
vendor base diversification, and inventory optimization. 
Further, the Company continuously monitors commodity 
prices and rigorously evaluates mitigation strategies during 
monthly management

review meetings.
Foreign Exchange Risk and Hedging: The Company 
operates within a dynamic economic environment 
and faces foreign exchange risks driven by currency 
fluctuations, primarily related to importing fuels, Capital 
goods and raw materials. To protect its financial interests 
against these adverse currency movements, the Company 
strictly adheres to a robust Risk Management Policy.
Applicability of SEBI Disclosures: Although the Company 
actively manages its commodity price risks through 
strategic sourcing and commercial negotiations, it does 
not currently possess material exposure to any commodity 
for which hedging instruments are actively traded in the 
financial derivative markets. As no direct commodity 
derivative hedging activities are carried out, the specific 
quantitative disclosures required under the applicable 
SEBI Circular regarding commodity derivative hedging are 
not applicable.

potential loss.

Inspected external legal opinions and other evidence 
to corroborate management's assessment of the risk 
profile in respect of legal claims and uncertain tax 
positions. 
•	
Engaged tax specialists to assess management’s 
application and interpretation of tax legislation affecting 
the Company, and to consider the quantification of 
exposures of Uncertain tax position and settlements 
arising from disputes with tax authorities in the various 
tax jurisdictions. 
•	
Assessed the relevant disclosures made within the 
standalone financial statements.
Revenue Recognition – Discounts, incentives, rebates etc.
(as described in note 27 of the standalone financial statements)
For the year ended March 31, 2026 the Company has 
recognized revenue from sale of goods of H 12,568.16 
Crores.
Revenue is measured net of discounts, incentives, rebates 
etc. earned by customers on the Company’s sales. 
Due to the Company’s presence across different marketing 
regions within the country and the competitive business 
environment, the estimation of the various types of 
discounts, incentives and rebate schemes to be re

cognised 
based on sales made during the year is material and 
considered to be complex and judgmental and dependent 
on various performance obligations and market conditions. 
Therefore, there is a risk of revenue being misstated as a 
result of inaccurate estimations over discounts, incentives 
and rebates.
Accordingly, given the complexity and judgement involved 
in the assessment of provisions required for discounts, 
incentives and rebates, Revenue recognition – Discounts, 
incentives, rebates etc. was determined to be a key audit 
matter in our audit of the Standalone financial statements.
Our audit procedures included the following:
•	
Considered Company’s revenue recognition policy and 
its compliance in terms of Ind AS 115 ‘Revenue from 
contracts with customers’.
•	
Assessed the design and tested the operating 
effectiveness of internal controls with regards to 
approvals, calculation, provision and disbursement of 
discounts, incentives and rebates.
•	
Performed sample test of supporting documentation 
for computation of discounts, incentives and rebates 
recorded and/or disbursed during the year including 
credit notes issued after the year end date. 
•	
Performed analytical review and compared the 
management’s assessment of discounts, incentives 
and rebates recorded for the current year with historical 
trends of discount given and reversal of such discounts, 
incentives and rebates to assess the appropriateness 
and adequacy of provisions made during the current 
year.
•	
Performed sample test of manual journals posted to 
discounts, incentives and rebates to identify unusual or 
irregular items.
•	
Assessed the relevant disclosures made within the 
standalone financial statements.

Financial Statements of J. K. Cement Limited 
Report on the Internal Financial Controls under 
Clause (i) of Sub-section 3 of Section 143 of 
the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”)
We have audited the internal financial controls with 
reference to standalone financial statements of J.K. 
Cement Limited (“the Company”) as of March 31, 2026 
in conjunction with our audit of the standalone financial 
statements of the Company for the year ended on that date.
Management’s Responsibility for Internal 
Financial Controls
The Company’s Management is responsible for 
establishing and maintaining internal financial controls 
based on the internal control over financial reporting 
criteria established by the Company considering the 
essential components of internal control stated in the 
Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls 
Over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute 
of Chartered Accountants of India (“ICAI”). These 
responsibilities include the design, implementation and 
maintenance of adequate internal financial controls that 
were operating effectively for ensuring the orderly and 
efficient conduct of its business, including adherence to 
the Company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, 
the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, 
the accuracy and completeness of the accounting 
records, and the timely preparation of reliable financial 
information, as required under the Companies Act, 2013.
Auditor’s Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the 
Company's internal financial controls with reference 
to these standalone financial statements based on our 
audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the 
Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls 
Over Financial Reporting (the “Guidance Note”) and 
the Standards on Auditing, as specified under section 
143(10) of the Act, to the extent applicable to an audit 
of internal financial controls, both issued by ICAI. Those 
Standards and the Guidance Note r

equire that we comply 
with ethical requirements and plan and perform the audit 
to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate 
internal financial controls with reference to these 
standalone financial statements was established and 
maintained and if such controls operated effectively in all 
material respects.
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain 
audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal 
financial controls with reference to these standalone 
financial statements and their operating effectiveness. 
Our audit of internal financial controls with reference 
to standalone financial statements included obtaining 
an understanding of internal financial controls with 
reference to these standalone financial statements, 
assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, 
and testing and evaluating the design and operating 
effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed 
risk. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s 
judgement, including the assessment of the risks of 
material misstatement of the financial statements, 
whether due to fraud or error.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is 
sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit 
opinion on the Company’s internal financial controls with 
reference to these standalone financial statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls With 
Reference to these Standalone Financial 
Statements
A company's internal financial controls with reference to 
standalone financial statements is a process designed 
to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability 
of financial reporting and the preparation of financial 
statements for external purposes in accordance with 
generally accepted accounting principles. A company's 
internal financial controls with reference to standalone 
financial statements includes those policies and 
procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of 
records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly 
reflect t

he transactions and dispositions of the assets 
of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance 
that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit 
preparation of financial statements in accordance 
with generally accepted accounting principles, and 
that receipts and expenditures of the company are 
being made only in accordance with authorisations of 
management and directors of the company; and (3) 
provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or 
timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or 
disposition of the company's assets that could have a 
material effect on the financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial 
Controls With Reference to Standalone 
Financial Statements
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial 
controls with reference to standalone financial 
statements, including the possibility of collusion or 
improper management override of controls, material 
misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not 
be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the 
internal financial controls with reference to standalone 
financial statements to future periods are subject to 
the risk that the internal financial control with reference 
to standalone financial statements may become 
inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the 
degree of compliance with the policies or procedures 
may deteriorate.
Opinion
In our opinion, the Company has, in all material respects, 
adequate internal financial controls with reference 
to standalone financial statements and such internal 
financial controls with reference to standalone 
financial statements were operating effectively as at 
March 31, 2026, based on the internal control over 
financial reporting criteria established by the Company 
considering the essential components of internal control 
stated in the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI.

II.	 Material Accounting Policies
	
The Company has consistently applied the following 
accounting policies to all periods presented in the 
financial statements.
	
1.	
Basis of preparation
	
	
The financial statements of the Company 
have been prepared in accordance with Indian 
Accounting Standards (Ind-AS) notified under 
the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 
Rules, 2015 (as amended from time to time) 
and presentation requirements of Division II of 
Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 (Ind 
AS compliant Schedule III). These financial 
statements are prepared under the historical 
cost convention on a going concern basis in 
accordance with IND AS.
	
	
These are Company’s separate 
financial statements.
	
	
The financial statements were approved for 
issue by the Board of Directors of the Company 
at their meeting held on 23.05.2026.
	
2.	 Basis of measurement
	
	
The financial statements have been prepared 
on a historical cost basis except the following 
assets and liabilities:
•	 Certain financial assets and liabilities that is 
measured at fair value (Refer note 41)
•	 Defined benefit lia

bility/(assets): fair value 
of plan assets less present value of defined 
benefit obligation (Refer note 39)
	
3.	
Functional and presentation currency
	
	
These financial statements are presented 
in Indian National Rupee (‘INR’), which is the 
Company’s functional currency. All amounts 
have been rounded to the nearest Crores 
up to two decimal places, except when 
otherwise indicated.
	
4.	
Use of judgements and estimates
	
	
The preparation of the financial statements 
requires management to make judgements, 
estimates and assumptions that affect the 
reported amounts of assets, liabilities, income, 
expenses, and the accompanying disclosures, 
and the disclosure of contingent assets and 
liabilities. Uncertainty about these assumptions 
and estimates could result in outcomes that 
require a material adjustment to the carrying 
amount of assets or liabilities affected in 
future periods.
	
	
Estimates and underlying assumptions are 
reviewed on an ongoing basis. Revisions to 
estimates are recognised prospectively.
	
A.	 Judgements
	
	
Information about the judgements made in 
applying accounting policies that have the 
most significant effects on the amounts 
recognised in the financial statements have 
been given below:
•	 Provision and contingencies
	
	
The assessment undertaken in recognizing 
provision and contingencies have been made 
in accordance with Ind AS 37, ‘Provisions, 
contingent liabilities and contingent assets’. 
The evaluation of the likelihood of the 
contingent events has required best judgement 
by management regarding the probability of 
exposure to potential loss.
	
B.	 Assumptions and estimation 
uncertainties
	
	
The key assumptions concerning the future and 
other key sources of estimation uncertainty 
at the reporting date, that have a significant 
risk of causing a material adjustment to the 
carrying amounts of assets and liabilities 
within the next financial year, are described 
below, the company based its assumptions and

estimates on parameters available when the 
financial statements were prepared. Existing 
circumstances and assumptions about future 
development, however, may change due to 
market change or circumstances arising that 
are beyond the control of the company. Such 
changes are reflected in the assumptions when 
they occurred.
	
	
Taxes:
	
	
Significant management judgement is required 
to determine the amount of deferred tax assets 
that can be recognised, based upon the likely 
timing and the level of future taxable profits 
together with future tax planning strategies.
	
	
To determine the future taxable profits, 
reference is made to the latest available profit 
forecasts. The Company is having MAT credit 
that may be used to offset taxable income.

extent it is probable that taxable profit will be

Useful lives of property, plant and equipment
	
	
The estimated useful lives of property, plant 
and equipment are based on a number of 
factors including the effects of obsolescence,

(such as the stability of the industry, and 
known technological advances) and the level of 
maintenance expenditure required to obtain the 
expected future cash flows from the asset. The 
Company reviews the useful life of property, 
plant and equipment at the end of each 
reportin

g date.
	
	
Post-retirement benefit plans
	
	
Employee benefit obligations (gratuity 
obligations) are determined using actuarial 
valuation. An actuarial valuation involves 
making various assumptions that may differ 
from actual developments in the future. These 
include the determination of the discount 
rates, future salary increases and Mortality 
rates. Due to the complexities involved in the 
valuation and its long term natures, a defined 
benefit obligation is highly sensitive to changes 
in these assumptions. All assumptions are 
reviewed at each reporting date.
	
	
Fair value measurement of financial 
instruments
	
	
The fair value of financial assets and financial 
liabilities recorded in the balance sheet in 
respect of which quoted prices in active 
markets are available and measured using 
valuation techniques. The inputs to these 
models are taken from observable markets 
where possible, but where this is not feasible, a 
degree of judgement is required in establishing 
fair values. Judgements include considerations 
of inputs such as liquidity risk, credit risk and 
volatility. Changes in assumptions about these 
factors could affect the reported fair value of 
financial instruments.
	
	
Leases - Estimating the incremental 
borrowing rate
	
	
The Company cannot readily determine the 
interest rate implicit in the lease, therefore, it 
uses its incremental borrowing rate (IBR) to 
measure lease liabilities. The IBR is the rate 
of interest that the Company would have to 
pay to borrow over a similar term, and with a 
similar security, the funds necessary to obtain 
an asset of a similar value to the right-of-use 
asset in a similar economic environment. The 
IBR therefore reflects what the Company ‘would 
have to pay’, which requires estimation when 
no observable rates are available or when 
they need to be adjusted to reflect the terms 
and conditions of the lease. The Company 
estimates the IBR using observable inputs (such 
as market interest

rates) when available.
	
	
Provision for expected credit losses of trade 
receivables
	
	
The Company makes provision of expected 
credit losses on trade receivables using 
a provision matrix. The provision matrix is 
based on its historical observed default rates, 
adjusted for forward looking estimates. At 
every reporting date, the historical observed 
default rates are updated, and Company makes 
appropriate provision wherever outstanding is 
for longer period and involves higher risk.
	
	
The assessment of the correlation between 
historical observed default rates, forecast 
economic conditions and ECLs is a significant 
estimate. The amount of ECLs is sensitive to 
changes in circumstances and of forecast 
economic conditions. The company’s 
historical credit loss experience and forecast 
of economic conditions may also not be 
representative of customer’s actual default in 
the future. The information about the ECLs on 
the company’s trade receivables and contract 
assets is disclosed in Note 41 (II) Financial risk 
management objective and policies
	
	
Provision for mines reclamation
	
	
The Company has recognised a provision for 
mines reclamation based on its best estimates. 
In determining the fair value of the provision, 
assumptions and estimates are made in relation 
to the expected future inflation rates, discount 
rate, expected cost of reclamation of mines, 
expected balance of reserves available in mines 
and the expected life of mines.
	
	
Litigations and contingencies
	
	
In the normal course of business, contingent 
liabilities may arise from litigation, taxation and 
other claims against the Company. A provision 
is recognised when the Company has a present 
obligation as a result of past events and it is 
probable that the Company will be required to 
settle that obligation. Where it is management’s 
assessment that the outcome cannot be 
reliably quantified or is uncertain, the claims 
are disclosed as contingent liabilities unless 
the

likelihood of an adverse outcome is remote. 
Such liabilities are disclosed in the notes but 
are not provided for in the financial statements. 
When considering the classification of legal 
or tax cases as probable, possible or remote, 
there is judgement involved. This pertains 
to the application of the legislation, which in 
certain cases is based upon management’s 
interpretation of specific applicable law, and 
the likelihood of settlement. Management uses 
in-house and external legal professionals to 
make informed decision. Although there can 
be no assurance regarding the final outcome 
of the legal proceedings, the Company does 
not expect them to have a materially adverse 
impact on the Company’s financial position 
or profitability.
	
5.	
Classification of Assets and Liabilities 
as Current and Non-Current
	
	
The Company present assets and liabilities 
in the balance sheet based on current/ non-
current classification. An asset is treated as 
current when it is:
•	 Expected to be realised or intended to 
be sold or consumed in normal operating 
cycle; or
•	 Held primarily for the purpose of trading; or
•	 Expected to be realised within twelve months 
after the reporting period; or
•	 Cash and cash equivalent unless restricted 
from being exchanged or used to settle a 
liability for at least twelve months after the 
reporting period.
	
	
All other assets are classified as non-current.
	
	
A liability is treated as current when:
•	 It is expected to be settled in normal 
operating cycle; or
•	 It is held primarily for the purpose of 
trading; or
•	 It is due to be settled within twelve months 
after the reporting period; or
•	 There is no unconditional right to defer the 
settlement of the liability for at least twelve 
months after the reporting period.
	
	
All other liabilities are classified as non-current.
	
	
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are classified 
as non-current assets and liabilities.
	
	
The operating cycle is the time between the

acquisition of the assets for processing and 
their realization in cash and cash equivalents. 
The Company has identified twelve months as 
its operating cycle.
	
6.	
Property, plant and equipment (PPE)
	
	
Recognition and measurement
	
	
Items of property, plant and equipment are 
stated at cost less accumulated depreciation 
and accumulated impairment loss, if any. The 
cost of assets comprises of purchase price 
and directly attributable cost of bringing the 
assets to working condition for its intended 
use including borrowing cost and incidental 
expenditure during construction incurred up 
to the date when the assets are ready to use. 
Capital work in progress includes cost of assets 
at sites, construction expenditure and interest 
on the funds deployed.
	
	
If significant parts of an item of property, plant 
and equipment have different useful lives, 
then they are accounted for as a separate 
item (major components) of property, plant 
and equipment.
	
	
Items such as spare parts, stand-by equipment 
and servicing equipment are recognized as 
property, plant and equipment when they 
meet the definition of property, plant and 
equipment. Otherwise, such items are classified 
as inventory.
	
	
An item of property, plant and equipment 
and any significant part initially recognised 
is derecognised upon disposal or when no 
future economic benefits are expected from 
its use or disposal. Any gain or loss arising 
on derecognition of the asset (calculated 
as the difference between the net disposal 
proceeds and the carrying amount of the asset) 
is included in the statement of profit and loss 
when the asset is derecognised.
	
	
Capital work in progress is stated at cost, net of 
accumulated impairment loss, if any.
	
	
Subsequent Measurement:
	
	
Subsequent expenditure is capitalised only if it 
is probable that the future economic benefits 
associated with the expenditure will flow to 
the Company.
